subject: accounting
description: Accounting question bank, FET (CAPS Grades 10-12). Keyed by atomic skill id. Each pool targets 20 items, FET pass mark 0.6, no timer. Cognitive mix per CAPS: ~30% Knowledge/Comprehension (difficulty 1), ~50% Application/Analysis (difficulty 2), ~20% Synthesis/Evaluation (difficulty 3). Tap-based mechanics only (no free-text / typed numbers), including the two Accounting-specific mechanics equation-effect (effect on Assets / Owner's equity / Liabilities) and double-entry (debit + credit accounts). Authored from data/accounting-authoring/grade{10,11,12}.mjs via scripts/gen-accounting-bank.mjs.

ACC.G10.T1.INFORMAL.A1.title: Informal vs formal bookkeeping
ACC.G10.T1.INFORMAL.A1.description: Comparison of the bookkeeping of the informal/indigenous sector and the formal sector: the concepts capital, fixed assets, stock, cost price, labour cost, selling price, income, expenses and profit; how resources are managed; and the process of determining selling prices, cost of sales, labour costs, income and expenses.
ACC.G10.T1.INFORMAL.A1.strand: Term 1 — Concepts, GAAP, control & bookkeeping of a sole trader
ACC.G10.T1.INFORMAL.A1.recovery_strategy: Profit = selling price − cost price. The informal trader still tracks the same things a formal business does, just without formal books.

questions.question: What do we call the money or goods the owner puts into a business to start it?
questions.memo: Capital is the owner's contribution to the business.

questions.question: Goods a business buys in order to sell them again are called…
questions.memo: Trading stock is bought to be resold at a profit.

questions.question: The price a business pays to buy an item is the…
questions.memo: Cost price is what the business pays; selling price is what the customer pays.

questions.question: The price the customer pays the business for an item is the…
questions.memo: Selling price is charged to the customer and is higher than cost price for a profit.

questions.question: Profit = selling price − ______.
questions.memo: Profit is what is left after the cost of the goods is covered.

questions.question: An informal trader who keeps no books still has capital, stock and profit.
questions.memo: Every business has these, whether or not formal records are kept.

questions.question: A loaf of bread is bought for R8 and sold for R12. The profit per loaf is…
questions.memo: Profit = R12 − R8 = R4.

questions.question: A trader buys 100 items at R5 each and sells them all at R9 each. The total profit is…
A trader pays a helper R200 for the day. To the business this is a…
questions.memo: Wages paid for work are a labour cost (an expense).

questions.question: Sort each item into what it is for a spaza shop.
questions.memo: Fixed assets are kept and used to trade; trading stock is bought to be sold.

questions.question: Sort each item into income or expense.
questions.memo: Income increases what the owner is worth; expenses are costs of running the business.

questions.question: Which of these is a fixed asset for a small trader?
options: A loaf of bread for sale
questions.memo: A fridge is kept and used in the business — a fixed asset.

questions.question: Selling price must be higher than cost price for the business to make a profit.
questions.memo: If selling price is below cost price the trader makes a loss.

questions.question: Cost price is R20 and the trader wants a profit of 50% on cost. The selling price is…
questions.memo: Profit = 50% × R20 = R10, so selling price = R20 + R10 = R30.

questions.question: In a month a trader sells goods for R5 000; those goods cost R3 200. The profit is…
The cost of the goods that were actually sold is called the ______.
questions.memo: Cost of sales is the cost price of the stock that was sold.

questions.question: Why is keeping no records a problem for an informal trader?
options: They cannot tell their true profit or track their money
questions.expected: They cannot tell their true profit or track their money
questions.memo: Without records the trader cannot measure profit or control cash.

questions.question: A formal business differs from an informal one mainly because it…
options: Keeps proper written records of its transactions
questions.expected: Keeps proper written records of its transactions
questions.memo: Formal businesses record transactions in books of account.

questions.question: Both informal and formal businesses use capital, earn income and incur expenses.
questions.memo: The concepts are the same; only the record-keeping differs.

questions.question: A trader keeps selling below cost price to attract customers. Over time this will…
questions.memo: Ongoing losses eat into the owner's capital.

ACC.G10.T1.ETHICS.A1.title: Code of ethics in the financial environment
ACC.G10.T1.ETHICS.A1.description: The code of ethics applicable to all parties in the financial environment and the basic principles of ethics: leadership, discipline, transparency, accountability, fairness, sustainability and responsible management. Ethics is integrated across all topics.
ACC.G10.T1.ETHICS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Concepts, GAAP, control & bookkeeping of a sole trader
ACC.G10.T1.ETHICS.A1.recovery_strategy: Tie each principle to a plain test: transparency = nothing hidden; accountability = answerable for your actions; fairness = same rules for all.

questions.question: A code of ethics is best described as…
options: A set of standards for honest, responsible behaviour
questions.expected: A set of standards for honest, responsible behaviour
questions.memo: A code of ethics guides how people should behave in the financial environment.

questions.question: Being open and hiding nothing about the finances is called…
questions.memo: Transparency means nothing is hidden.

questions.question: Being answerable for your actions and decisions is called…
questions.memo: Accountability means you can be held responsible for what you do.

questions.question: Treating all parties equally and without bias is called…
questions.memo: Fairness means the same rules apply to everyone.

questions.question: Ethics matters only for big companies, not for small traders.
questions.memo: Ethics applies to every party in the financial environment.

questions.question: Using resources so that they last for the future is called ______.
questions.memo: Sustainability means meeting today's needs without harming the future.

questions.question: A bookkeeper deliberately hides a loss from the owner. Which principle is broken?
questions.memo: Hiding information breaks transparency.

questions.question: A manager awards a contract to his brother who charged the most. Which principle is broken?
questions.memo: Favouring family over the best offer is unfair.

questions.question: An employee takes cash and cannot explain where it went. Which principle is broken?
questions.memo: Being unable to account for money breaks accountability.

questions.question: Match each action to the principle it shows.

items.text: Signing for the payments you approved
Showing all the notes to the statements
Giving every supplier the same chance to quote

questions.memo: Each action demonstrates a single ethical principle in practice.

questions.question: Responsible management means using the business's money and assets carefully.
questions.memo: Responsible management looks after the resources entrusted to it.

questions.question: Which behaviour is ethical?
options: Recording all income honestly, even cash sales
Leaving cash sales out of the books
questions.expected: Recording all income honestly, even cash sales
questions.memo: All income must be recorded, including cash.

questions.question: A supplier offers a bribe to win a contract. The ethical response is to…
questions.memo: Bribery is unethical and should be refused and reported.

questions.question: Disciplined financial behaviour means…
options: Following the rules and procedures consistently
Changing the rules to suit yourself
questions.expected: Following the rules and procedures consistently
questions.memo: Discipline is sticking to the correct procedures.

questions.question: Build a short answer explaining why transparency matters.
questions.prompt: Why does transparency matter in a business?

options.text: Transparency means the finances are open and nothing is hidden
Transparency means the business makes the most profit
Owners and SARS can see the true income and expenses
Customers get cheaper prices
So stakeholders can trust the figures and make good decisions
So the business can hide losses

questions.memo: A good point-evidence-explanation links transparency to trustworthy decisions.

questions.question: Strong ethical leadership in a business mainly…
options: Sets the example that others follow
questions.expected: Sets the example that others follow
questions.memo: Leaders set the ethical tone for everyone else.

questions.question: Sustainability includes caring for the environment and community, not just profit.
questions.memo: Sustainability balances profit with social and environmental responsibility.

questions.question: Deliberately hiding tax owed to SARS breaks mainly which principles?
questions.memo: Hiding tax is dishonest and unaccountable.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a basic principle of ethics?
questions.memo: Profit at any cost is the opposite of ethical behaviour.

questions.question: Sort each action as ethical or unethical.
questions.memo: Ethical actions are honest and fair; unethical actions deceive or exploit.

ACC.G10.T1.GAAP.A1.title: GAAP principles
ACC.G10.T1.GAAP.A1.description: Definition and application of the Generally Accepted Accounting Practice principles: historical cost, prudence, materiality, business entity rule, going concern and matching. Applied to all relevant topics.
ACC.G10.T1.GAAP.A1.strand: Term 1 — Concepts, GAAP, control & bookkeeping of a sole trader
ACC.G10.T1.GAAP.A1.recovery_strategy: Business entity = the owner and the business are separate. Going concern = the business will keep operating. Matching = record income with the expenses that earned it.

questions.question: Recording assets at the price actually paid for them is the ______ principle.
questions.memo: Historical cost records assets at their original purchase price.

questions.question: Keeping the owner's private money separate from the business is the ______ rule.
questions.memo: The business entity rule treats the business as separate from its owner.

questions.question: Assuming the business will keep operating into the future is ______.
questions.memo: Going concern assumes continued operation.

questions.question: Being cautious and not overstating profit or assets is ______.
questions.memo: Prudence avoids overstating the position.

questions.question: Recording income in the same period as the expenses that earned it is the ______ principle.
questions.memo: Matching links income to the expenses incurred to earn it.

questions.question: Ignoring very small amounts that would not affect a decision is ______.
questions.memo: Materiality means only significant amounts need special treatment.

questions.question: The owner pays his home electricity from the business bank account. Which principle is broken?
questions.memo: Private expenses must not be mixed with the business.

questions.question: A building bought 10 years ago for R500 000, now worth R2 000 000, is still shown at R500 000. Which principle?
questions.memo: Assets stay at original cost under historical cost.

questions.question: A possible large lawsuit loss is provided for, but a possible gain is not recorded. Which principle?
questions.memo: Prudence records likely losses but not uncertain gains.

questions.question: Writing off a R5 stapler as an expense instead of a fixed asset uses the ______ principle.
questions.memo: The amount is too small to capitalise — it is immaterial.

questions.question: Match each example to the GAAP principle it shows.

items.text: An asset shown at the price paid
Preparing next year's budget assuming the business continues
This year's rent recorded against this year's income
Stock recorded at what it cost
Buying new equipment expecting future use
Depreciation spread over the asset's useful life

questions.memo: Each example illustrates exactly one GAAP principle.

questions.question: Going concern assumes the business will close down soon.
questions.memo: Going concern assumes the OPPOSITE — continued operation.

questions.question: Why is the business entity rule important?
options: So business results are not mixed with the owner's private affairs
So the business pays no tax
questions.expected: So business results are not mixed with the owner's private affairs
questions.memo: It keeps the business's financial picture clean and separate.

questions.question: Spreading the cost of a vehicle over its useful life through depreciation is an example of…
questions.memo: Depreciation matches the asset's cost to the periods that benefit.

questions.question: Two bookkeepers value the same uncertain debt differently. Decide which source each statement fits.

source_a.text: Source A: provides for a doubtful debt because the customer may not pay.

source_b.text: Source B: records the full debt as certain to be received.

statements.text: Ignores prudence and may overstate assets
Is recording a transaction about a debtor

questions.memo: Source A is prudent; Source B overstates by ignoring the risk.

questions.question: Being cautious so that profit and assets are not overstated is called ______.
questions.memo: Prudence keeps the figures cautious and realistic.

questions.question: Which principle allows a business to write off a cheap calculator immediately?
questions.memo: Small, immaterial items can be expensed at once.

questions.question: Under historical cost, assets are revalued to market price every year.
questions.memo: Historical cost keeps assets at original cost, not market value.

questions.question: A business is about to be liquidated. Which assumption no longer holds?
questions.memo: If the business is closing, going concern falls away.

questions.question: Which principle ensures expenses are recorded with the income they helped to earn?
questions.memo: Matching aligns expenses with the related income.

ACC.G10.T1.CONTROL.A1.title: Internal control basics
ACC.G10.T1.CONTROL.A1.description: What internal control means and the basic internal control processes: control environment, risk assessment, control activities supported by policy and procedures, information and communication, and monitoring of performance. Integrated with other topics.
ACC.G10.T1.CONTROL.A1.strand: Term 1 — Concepts, GAAP, control & bookkeeping of a sole trader
ACC.G10.T1.CONTROL.A1.recovery_strategy: Division of duties, authorisation, and physical controls are control ACTIVITIES. Spotting what could go wrong is risk ASSESSMENT.

questions.question: Internal control is best described as…
options: The system a business uses to protect its assets and records
questions.expected: The system a business uses to protect its assets and records
questions.memo: Internal control safeguards assets and ensures reliable records.

questions.question: Splitting duties so one person does not handle a whole transaction alone is called…
questions.memo: Division of duties reduces the chance of error and fraud.

questions.question: Good internal control helps prevent theft and errors.
questions.memo: That is exactly what internal control is for.

questions.question: Counting the cash in the till at the end of each day is an example of…
questions.memo: A daily cash count is a control activity (a physical check).

questions.question: Identifying what could go wrong in the business is called…
questions.memo: Risk assessment spots the threats the controls must address.

questions.question: Checking that the controls are actually working over time is called ______.
questions.memo: Monitoring reviews whether controls keep working.

questions.question: A shop installs cameras and keeps cash in a locked safe. These are…
questions.memo: Cameras and safes physically protect assets.

questions.question: Why should the person who receives cash NOT also record it in the books?
options: To reduce the chance of theft going unnoticed
questions.expected: To reduce the chance of theft going unnoticed
questions.memo: Separating the roles makes hidden theft harder.

questions.question: Sort each example into the correct internal control process.

items.text: Noticing that cash handling could be stolen
Requiring two signatures on a cheque

questions.memo: Spotting threats is risk assessment; doing something about them is a control activity.

questions.question: Requiring a manager to authorise large payments is a control activity.
questions.memo: Authorisation is a key control activity.

questions.question: Pre-numbered receipts help internal control because…
options: Missing numbers reveal a missing transaction
questions.expected: Missing numbers reveal a missing transaction
questions.memo: Sequential numbering makes gaps easy to spot.

questions.question: Which is a good internal control over stock?
options: Regular stock counts compared to records
Letting any worker take stock freely
questions.expected: Regular stock counts compared to records
questions.memo: Comparing counts to records detects loss or theft.

questions.question: An environment where management values honesty and sets clear rules is the…
questions.memo: The control environment is the overall tone set by management.

questions.question: Passing information clearly between staff so controls work is part of ______ and communication.
questions.memo: Information and communication systems support the controls.

questions.question: Internal control should be integrated with the business's other activities, not done separately.
questions.memo: Control works best built into everyday processes.

questions.question: A weakness in internal control is…
options: One person controls cash, recording and banking
Two signatures are needed on cheques
questions.expected: One person controls cash, recording and banking
questions.memo: No division of duties is a serious weakness.

questions.question: Good internal control mainly benefits the business by…
options: Protecting assets and giving reliable information
Removing the need for an owner
questions.expected: Protecting assets and giving reliable information
questions.memo: Reliable records and safe assets are the core benefits.

questions.question: Sort each into a strength or weakness of internal control.

items.text: No one checks the petty cash

questions.memo: Strengths protect assets; weaknesses leave gaps for error or fraud.

questions.question: Why does management 'monitor' the controls?
options: To make sure they keep working as the business changes
questions.expected: To make sure they keep working as the business changes
questions.memo: Monitoring keeps controls effective over time.

questions.question: Setting policies and procedures supports the control activities of a business.
questions.memo: Policies and procedures direct how controls are applied.

ACC.G10.T1.CONCEPTS.A1.title: Accounting concepts & the accounting cycle
ACC.G10.T1.CONCEPTS.A1.description: Definition of accounting concepts up to financial statements — debit, credit, equity, capital, assets, liabilities, ledger, journal, profit, loss, VAT, income, expenses, final accounts, financial statements, discounts, the accounting cycle, financial vs managerial accounting and the perpetual inventory system.
ACC.G10.T1.CONCEPTS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Concepts, GAAP, control & bookkeeping of a sole trader
ACC.G10.T1.CONCEPTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Assets are what the business owns/controls; liabilities are what it owes; income increases equity; expenses decrease it.

questions.question: Things the business owns or controls and uses to trade are called…
questions.memo: Assets are resources owned/controlled by the business.

questions.question: Amounts the business owes to others are called…
questions.memo: Liabilities are debts the business must pay.

questions.question: The owner's interest in the business (capital) is also called…
questions.memo: Owner's equity is the owner's claim on the assets.

questions.question: Money the owner takes out of the business for private use is called…
questions.memo: Drawings reduce owner's equity.

questions.question: The left side of an account is the ______ side.
questions.memo: Debit is the left side; credit is the right side.

questions.question: Income increases owner's equity and expenses decrease it.
questions.memo: Profit (income less expenses) flows into owner's equity.

questions.question: Sort each item as an asset or a liability.
questions.memo: Assets are owned; liabilities are owed.

questions.question: Sort each account as income or expense.
questions.memo: Income is earned; expenses are costs of operating.

questions.question: A debtor is…
options: Someone who owes the business money
questions.expected: Someone who owes the business money
questions.memo: Debtors owe the business (an asset).

questions.question: A creditor is…
options: Someone who owes the business money
questions.memo: Creditors are owed by the business (a liability).

questions.question: Which shows the correct order of the accounting cycle?
options: Source document → journal → ledger → trial balance → financial statements
Ledger → journal → source document → financial statements
Trial balance → source document → journal → ledger
Financial statements → ledger → journal → source document
questions.expected: Source document → journal → ledger → trial balance → financial statements
questions.memo: The cycle starts with the source document and ends with the statements.

questions.question: A discount a business gives a customer for paying quickly is a…
questions.memo: Discount allowed is given to debtors.

questions.question: A discount a business receives from a supplier for paying quickly is a…
questions.memo: Discount received is income from suppliers.

questions.question: Under the ______ inventory system, the Trading Stock account is updated with every purchase and sale.
questions.memo: The perpetual system tracks stock continuously.

questions.question: Financial Accounting is mainly concerned with…
options: Reporting past results to outside parties
questions.expected: Reporting past results to outside parties
questions.memo: Financial accounting reports historical results externally.

questions.question: Managerial Accounting is mainly concerned with…
options: Providing information for internal planning and decisions
questions.expected: Providing information for internal planning and decisions
questions.memo: Managerial accounting helps managers plan and decide.

questions.question: A trial balance is prepared to check that total debits equal total credits.
questions.memo: The trial balance tests the equality of debits and credits.

questions.question: Which list places items in the right groups?
options: Assets: vehicles, stock; Liabilities: loan, creditors
Assets: loan, creditors; Liabilities: vehicles, stock
questions.expected: Assets: vehicles, stock; Liabilities: loan, creditors
questions.memo: Vehicles and stock are owned; loans and creditors are owed.

questions.question: Final accounts (Trading and Profit and Loss accounts) are prepared in order to…
options: Determine the profit or loss for the period
questions.expected: Determine the profit or loss for the period
questions.memo: Final accounts work out profit or loss.

questions.question: Which best explains 'liabilities'?
options: Present obligations the business must settle in future
questions.expected: Present obligations the business must settle in future
questions.memo: Liabilities are what the business owes.

ACC.G10.T1.SOURCEDOCS.A1.title: Source documents & double entry
ACC.G10.T1.SOURCEDOCS.A1.description: The source documents that start each transaction and the double-entry principle — every transaction has an equal debit and credit. Links each document to the journal it feeds.
ACC.G10.T1.SOURCEDOCS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Concepts, GAAP, control & bookkeeping of a sole trader
ACC.G10.T1.SOURCEDOCS.A1.recovery_strategy: Every transaction has TWO sides — one debit and one credit of equal value. If both are on the same side, it cannot balance.

questions.question: The source document for cash received is a…
questions.memo: A receipt is issued when cash is received.

questions.question: Goods sold on credit are supported by the…
questions.memo: The seller keeps a duplicate invoice for a credit sale.

questions.question: Goods returned by a credit customer are supported by a…
questions.memo: A credit note records goods returned by a debtor.

questions.question: Every transaction recorded in the books should be supported by a source document.
questions.memo: Source documents are the proof behind each entry.

questions.question: The double-entry principle means every transaction has one debit and one ______ of equal value.
questions.memo: Debits must always equal credits.

questions.question: Money paid into the bank is supported by a…
questions.memo: A deposit slip proves money banked.

questions.question: Match each source document to its transaction.
questions.memo: Each document supports a specific kind of transaction.

questions.question: The business makes a cash sale of goods. Choose the debit and credit accounts.
questions.memo: Cash sale: Bank increases (debit), Sales increases (credit).

questions.question: The owner deposits R50 000 of personal money to start the business.
questions.memo: Capital contribution: Bank (debit), Capital (credit).

questions.question: The business pays rent by EFT.
questions.memo: Rent expense (debit) increases; Bank (credit) decreases.

questions.question: The business buys equipment and pays by EFT.
questions.memo: Equipment (debit) increases; Bank (credit) decreases.

questions.question: The business receives a loan from the bank.
questions.memo: Loan received: Bank (debit), Loan (credit).

questions.question: The owner takes R1 000 cash from the business for private use.
questions.memo: Drawings (debit); Bank (credit) decreases.

questions.question: For every debit entry there must be…
questions.memo: Double entry keeps debits and credits equal.

questions.question: A cash invoice is the source document for a cash sale.
questions.memo: A cash invoice/receipt supports a cash sale.

questions.question: Which document-and-journal pair is correct?
questions.memo: Receipts feed the Cash Receipts Journal.

questions.question: If only one side of a transaction is recorded, the Trial Balance will…
questions.memo: A one-sided entry breaks the debit = credit rule.

questions.question: The business pays a supplier (creditor) by EFT.
questions.memo: Paying a creditor: Creditors control (debit) decreases; Bank (credit) decreases.

questions.question: The business receives cash from a debtor settling their account.
questions.memo: Debtor pays: Bank (debit) increases; Debtors control (credit) decreases.

questions.question: Why does a business keep source documents?
options: They provide proof and detail of each transaction
questions.expected: They provide proof and detail of each transaction
questions.memo: Source documents are the evidence for every entry.

ACC.G10.T1.CASHJOURNALS.A1.title: Cash journals (CRJ, CPJ, Petty Cash)
ACC.G10.T1.CASHJOURNALS.A1.description: Recording cash transactions in the Cash Receipts Journal, Cash Payments Journal (including loans, fixed deposits, interest income and expense, dishonoured cheques, discount allowed and received) and Petty Cash Journal.
ACC.G10.T1.CASHJOURNALS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Concepts, GAAP, control & bookkeeping of a sole trader
ACC.G10.T1.CASHJOURNALS.A1.recovery_strategy: Money IN → Cash Receipts Journal. Money OUT → Cash Payments Journal. Small cash payments → Petty Cash Journal.

questions.question: Cash received is recorded in the…
questions.memo: Money coming in is recorded in the CRJ.

questions.question: Cash paid out is recorded in the…
questions.memo: Money going out is recorded in the CPJ.

questions.question: Small everyday cash payments are recorded in the…
questions.memo: Petty cash handles small payments.

questions.question: A discount granted to a debtor who pays promptly is discount ______.
questions.memo: Discount allowed is given to customers.

questions.question: Interest received on a fixed deposit is recorded in the Cash Receipts Journal.
questions.memo: Interest received is cash coming in — CRJ.

questions.question: Bank charges and interest on an overdraft are recorded in the…
questions.memo: Bank charges reduce the bank balance — CPJ.

questions.question: Record a cash sale of goods. Choose the debit and credit accounts.
questions.memo: Cash sale: Bank (debit), Sales (credit).

questions.question: Wages are paid to workers in cash.
questions.memo: Wages (debit) increases; Bank (credit) decreases.

questions.question: Stationery is bought using petty cash.
questions.memo: Stationery (debit); Petty cash (credit) decreases.

questions.question: The total of the Bank column in the Cash Receipts Journal is posted to the…
options: Debit side of the Bank account
Credit side of the Bank account
questions.expected: Debit side of the Bank account
questions.memo: Receipts increase the bank — posted to the debit of Bank.

questions.question: A business pays a creditor and receives a settlement discount. The discount received is…
questions.memo: Discount received is income to the business.

questions.question: Money paid into a fixed deposit is recorded in the ______.
questions.memo: Investing cash in a fixed deposit is a payment out of bank — CPJ.

questions.question: The business receives interest on its current bank account.
questions.memo: Interest received: Bank (debit), Interest income (credit).

questions.question: Which transaction does NOT belong in the Cash Receipts Journal?
options: A debtor settling their account in cash
questions.memo: Paying rent is a payment — it belongs in the CPJ.

questions.question: Which is the correct order for handling a cash receipt?
options: Receive cash → issue receipt → record in CRJ → post to ledger
Post to ledger → record in CRJ → issue receipt → receive cash
Record in CRJ → receive cash → post to ledger → issue receipt
Issue receipt → post to ledger → record in CRJ → receive cash
questions.expected: Receive cash → issue receipt → record in CRJ → post to ledger
questions.memo: The flow runs document → journal → ledger.

questions.question: Trading stock is bought for cash (perpetual inventory system).
questions.memo: Cash purchase of stock: Trading stock (debit), Bank (credit).

questions.question: The Petty Cash Journal helps keep small payments out of the main Cash Payments Journal.
questions.memo: Petty cash reduces clutter from many tiny payments.

questions.question: At month-end the CRJ and CPJ bank totals are used to…
options: Update the Bank account in the General Ledger
questions.expected: Update the Bank account in the General Ledger
questions.memo: The journal totals post to the Bank account.

questions.question: Discount allowed reduces the amount of cash the business actually receives from a debtor.
questions.memo: The debtor pays less because of the discount allowed.

questions.question: A dishonoured (R/D) cheque previously received from a debtor is recorded by…
options: Reducing the bank and reinstating the debtor
questions.expected: Reducing the bank and reinstating the debtor
questions.memo: The bounced cheque cancels the earlier receipt; the debtor owes again.

ACC.G10.T1.CREDITJOURNALS.A1.title: Credit journals (DJ, DAJ, CJ, CAJ, GJ)
ACC.G10.T1.CREDITJOURNALS.A1.description: Recording credit transactions in the Debtors' Journal, Debtors' Allowances Journal, Creditors' Journal and Creditors' Allowances Journal, and the General Journal entries for bad debts, interest on overdue accounts, cancellations of discount on dishonoured cheques and corrections of errors.
ACC.G10.T1.CREDITJOURNALS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Concepts, GAAP, control & bookkeeping of a sole trader
ACC.G10.T1.CREDITJOURNALS.A1.recovery_strategy: Sold goods on credit → Debtors' Journal. Bought goods on credit → Creditors' Journal. Returns reverse into the matching Allowances journal.

questions.question: Goods sold on credit are recorded in the…
questions.memo: Credit sales go in the Debtors' Journal.

questions.question: Goods bought on credit are recorded in the…
questions.memo: Credit purchases of stock go in the Creditors' Journal.

questions.question: Goods returned by a credit customer are recorded in the…
questions.memo: Customer returns go in the Debtors' Allowances Journal.

questions.question: Goods returned to a credit supplier are recorded in the…
questions.memo: Returns to suppliers go in the Creditors' Allowances Journal.

questions.question: A debt that will not be paid and is written off is a ______ debt.
questions.memo: An uncollectable debt is written off as a bad debt.

questions.question: The General Journal records transactions that do not fit the other journals.
questions.memo: The General Journal handles the 'other' entries.

questions.question: The business sells goods on credit to a customer.
questions.memo: Credit sale: Debtors control (debit), Sales (credit).

questions.question: The business buys trading stock on credit (perpetual system).
questions.memo: Credit purchase: Trading stock (debit), Creditors control (credit).

questions.question: A bad debt owed by a debtor is written off.
questions.memo: Writing off a bad debt: Bad debts (debit), Debtors control (credit).

questions.question: Match each transaction to its journal.
questions.memo: Each credit transaction has its own subsidiary journal.

questions.question: Interest charged to a debtor on an overdue account is recorded in the…
questions.memo: Interest on overdue accounts is a General Journal entry.

questions.question: The Debtors' Journal total for the month is posted to the credit of…
questions.memo: Total credit sales are credited to Sales.

questions.question: Goods returned by a customer reduce the amount owed by the ______.
questions.memo: Returns reduce the debtor's balance.

questions.question: A correction of an error in the books is usually done through the…
questions.memo: Error corrections are processed in the General Journal.

questions.question: Buying a vehicle on credit is recorded in the Creditors' Journal.
questions.memo: The Creditors' Journal is for trading stock; a vehicle on credit goes in the General Journal.

questions.question: Buying goods on credit increases both…
questions.memo: Stock rises and the amount owed to suppliers rises.

questions.question: A bad debt written off in a past year is later recovered. This is recorded as…
questions.memo: Recovering a written-off debt is income.

questions.question: A credit customer returns goods previously sold to them.
questions.memo: Customer returns: Debtors' allowances (debit), Debtors control (credit).

questions.question: Why keep separate Debtors' and Creditors' journals?
options: To group similar credit transactions for easy posting and control
questions.expected: To group similar credit transactions for easy posting and control
questions.memo: Grouping makes posting and control simpler.

questions.question: A credit note issued to a customer supports an entry in the Debtors' Allowances Journal.
questions.memo: The credit note is the source document for customer returns.

ACC.G10.T1.LEDGERS.A1.title: Posting to ledgers, Trial Balance & control lists
ACC.G10.T1.LEDGERS.A1.description: Posting journals to the General, Debtors' and Creditors' Ledgers, drawing up a Trial Balance, and preparing debtors' and creditors' lists to reconcile with the control accounts (including correcting errors and omissions).
ACC.G10.T1.LEDGERS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Concepts, GAAP, control & bookkeeping of a sole trader
ACC.G10.T1.LEDGERS.A1.recovery_strategy: The Trial Balance debit total must equal the credit total. The debtors'/creditors' list total must equal its control account balance.

questions.question: Accounts such as Bank, Sales and Capital are kept in the…
questions.memo: The General Ledger holds the main accounts.

questions.question: Individual customer accounts are kept in the…
questions.memo: Each debtor has an account in the Debtors' Ledger.

questions.question: Individual supplier accounts are kept in the…
questions.memo: Each creditor has an account in the Creditors' Ledger.

questions.question: A list of all the ledger balances used to check that debits equal credits is the ______.
questions.memo: The Trial Balance tests debit = credit.

questions.question: The Debtors' Control account balance should equal the total of the Debtors' List.
questions.memo: The control account summarises the individual debtors.

questions.question: Sort each account by the side it normally balances on.
questions.memo: Assets and expenses are debit; liabilities, income and capital are credit.

questions.question: The Sales account normally has a…
questions.memo: Income accounts carry a credit balance.

questions.question: A favourable Bank balance is shown as a…
questions.memo: A positive bank balance is a debit (asset) balance.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of steps?
options: Record in journal → post to ledger → balance the account → prepare trial balance
Prepare trial balance → post to ledger → record in journal → balance
Balance the account → record in journal → post to ledger → trial balance
Post to ledger → prepare trial balance → record in journal → balance
questions.expected: Record in journal → post to ledger → balance the account → prepare trial balance
questions.memo: Entries flow from journal to ledger to trial balance.

questions.question: The Debtors' List totals R8 500 but the Debtors' Control account shows R8 700. This means…
options: There is an error or omission to find
The business made a profit of R200
questions.expected: There is an error or omission to find
questions.memo: A difference signals an error to be located and corrected.

questions.question: The Creditors' Control account is kept in the ______ Ledger.
questions.memo: The control account sits in the General Ledger; individual creditors in the Creditors' Ledger.

questions.question: The Capital account normally has a…
questions.memo: Owner's equity carries a credit balance.

questions.question: A debit balance on the Bank account means the business has money in the bank.
questions.memo: A debit (favourable) bank balance means funds are available.

questions.question: 'Posting' means…
options: Transferring entries from the journals to the ledger accounts
questions.expected: Transferring entries from the journals to the ledger accounts
questions.memo: Posting moves journal entries into the ledger.

questions.question: The Trial Balance does not balance. The most likely cause is…
options: A one-sided posting or arithmetic error
questions.expected: A one-sided posting or arithmetic error
questions.memo: Imbalance usually points to a one-sided entry or maths error.

questions.question: Place each account in the correct ledger.
questions.memo: Customers go to the Debtors' Ledger, suppliers to the Creditors' Ledger, the rest to the General Ledger.

questions.question: Why reconcile the Debtors' List to the Control account?
options: To confirm the individual accounts agree with the total owed
questions.expected: To confirm the individual accounts agree with the total owed
questions.memo: Reconciliation confirms the detail matches the summary.

questions.question: In the Trial Balance, total debits must equal total ______.
questions.memo: The two columns must be equal.

questions.question: An Equipment account normally has a…
questions.memo: Assets carry a debit balance.

questions.question: The Trial Balance is an internal check, not a financial statement given to outsiders.
questions.memo: It is a working tool, not a published statement.

ACC.G10.T1.EQUATION.A1.title: The accounting equation
ACC.G10.T1.EQUATION.A1.description: Analysing transactions of a sole trader and showing their effect on the accounting equation (Assets = Owner's equity + Liabilities) for all transactions up to financial statements.
ACC.G10.T1.EQUATION.A1.strand: Term 1 — Concepts, GAAP, control & bookkeeping of a sole trader
ACC.G10.T1.EQUATION.A1.recovery_strategy: Every transaction keeps A = OE + L in balance. If assets go up, something else must change by the same amount.

questions.question: The owner invests cash as capital into the business.
questions.memo: Bank (asset) up; Capital (owner's equity) up; no liability change.

questions.question: The business pays the monthly rent by EFT.
questions.memo: Bank (asset) down; the expense reduces owner's equity; no liability change.

questions.question: The business renders a service and receives R500 cash.
questions.memo: Bank (asset) up; income increases owner's equity; no liability change.

questions.question: The business buys equipment and pays cash. (Hint: one asset replaces another.)
questions.memo: Equipment up and Bank down by the same amount — total assets, equity and liabilities are unchanged.

questions.question: The business takes out a bank loan, received in the bank.
questions.memo: Bank (asset) up; loan (liability) up; equity unchanged.

questions.question: The business repays part of its loan by EFT.
questions.memo: Bank (asset) down; loan (liability) down; equity unchanged.

questions.question: The owner takes R1 000 cash as drawings.
questions.memo: Bank (asset) down; drawings reduce owner's equity; no liability change.

questions.question: The business buys trading stock and pays cash (perpetual system).
questions.memo: Trading stock up and Bank down by the same amount — totals unchanged.

questions.question: The business buys trading stock on credit.
questions.memo: Trading stock (asset) up; creditors (liability) up; equity unchanged.

questions.question: The business pays a creditor by EFT.
questions.memo: Bank (asset) down; creditors (liability) down; equity unchanged.

questions.question: A debtor settles their account in cash.
questions.memo: Bank up and debtors down by the same amount — total assets unchanged.

questions.question: Depreciation is written off on equipment.
questions.memo: The asset's carrying value (asset) falls; depreciation is an expense reducing equity.

questions.question: The business receives interest on a fixed deposit, paid into the bank.
questions.memo: Bank (asset) up; interest income increases equity; no liability change.

questions.question: Which transaction increases an asset and a liability by the same amount?
options: A cash sale of a service
questions.memo: Stock (asset) and creditors (liability) both rise.

questions.question: The accounting equation is…
questions.memo: This is the fundamental accounting equation.

questions.question: The owner invests cash capital. Choose the debit and credit accounts.
questions.memo: Capital: Bank (debit), Capital (credit).

questions.question: The business buys a vehicle on credit.
questions.memo: Vehicle on credit: Vehicles (debit), Creditors control (credit).

questions.question: Paying an expense in cash affects the equation by…
questions.memo: Cash (asset) falls and the expense reduces equity.

questions.question: A debtor's account is written off as a bad debt.
questions.memo: Debtors (asset) fall; the bad debt is an expense reducing equity; no liability change.

questions.question: Why must the accounting equation always balance?
options: Every transaction has equal debit and credit effects
The business always makes a profit
Assets are always bigger than liabilities
questions.expected: Every transaction has equal debit and credit effects
questions.memo: Double entry keeps the equation in balance.

ACC.G10.T2.VAT.A1.title: VAT basics
ACC.G10.T2.VAT.A1.description: The basic concepts of Value-Added Tax: the need for, purpose of and principles of VAT, zero-rated items, VAT-exempt items, standard-rated (VAT-able) items and the current VAT rate.
ACC.G10.T2.VAT.A1.strand: Term 2 — VAT, salaries & wages, adjustments & final accounts
ACC.G10.T2.VAT.A1.recovery_strategy: Zero-rated = taxed at 0% (e.g. brown bread, maize meal). Exempt = outside VAT (e.g. some financial services). Standard-rated = the current VAT rate.

questions.question: VAT stands for…
questions.memo: VAT is Value-Added Tax.

questions.question: The current standard VAT rate in South Africa is…
questions.memo: The standard rate is 15%.

questions.question: Businesses collect VAT on behalf of…
questions.memo: VAT is collected for the South African Revenue Service.

questions.question: Basic foods such as brown bread and maize meal are ______-rated for VAT.
questions.memo: Basic foods are zero-rated (taxed at 0%).

questions.question: A business adds VAT to the selling price of standard-rated goods.
questions.memo: Standard-rated sales include 15% VAT.

questions.question: Goods taxed at 0% VAT are called…
questions.memo: Zero-rated supplies are taxed at 0%.

questions.question: Which is a zero-rated item?
questions.memo: Maize meal is a zero-rated basic food.

questions.question: Which is usually a VAT-exempt supply?
questions.memo: Residential accommodation is VAT-exempt.

questions.question: Sort each supply by its VAT treatment.
questions.memo: Zero-rated = 0% (basic foods); standard = 15%; exempt = outside VAT.

questions.question: VAT a business charges on its sales is called…
questions.memo: Output VAT is charged on sales.

questions.question: VAT a business pays on its purchases (and can claim back) is called…
questions.memo: Input VAT is paid on purchases and claimed back.

questions.question: The main purpose of VAT is to raise ______ for the government.
questions.memo: VAT is a source of government revenue.

questions.question: Zero-rated and exempt supplies are exactly the same thing.
questions.memo: They differ: zero-rated vendors can claim input VAT, exempt cannot.

questions.question: A registered VAT vendor must…
options: Charge VAT and pay it over to SARS
Keep all the VAT as profit
Charge VAT but never pay SARS
questions.expected: Charge VAT and pay it over to SARS
questions.memo: Vendors collect VAT and remit it to SARS.

questions.question: VAT is an example of a/an…
questions.memo: VAT is an indirect tax on consumption.

questions.question: A business NOT registered for VAT…
options: Cannot charge VAT or claim input VAT
questions.expected: Cannot charge VAT or claim input VAT
questions.memo: Only registered vendors deal in VAT.

questions.question: VAT increases the final price the consumer pays.
questions.memo: The consumer ultimately bears the VAT.

questions.question: Why are basic foods zero-rated?
options: To ease the burden on poorer households
questions.expected: To ease the burden on poorer households
questions.memo: Zero-rating basics keeps essential food affordable.

questions.question: The key difference between zero-rated and exempt supplies is that…
options: Zero-rated vendors can claim input VAT; exempt vendors cannot
questions.expected: Zero-rated vendors can claim input VAT; exempt vendors cannot
questions.memo: Input-VAT recovery is the practical difference.

questions.question: Sort each by whether 15% VAT is charged on it.
questions.memo: Standard-rated items carry 15%; zero-rated and exempt items do not.

ACC.G10.T2.SALARIES.A1.title: Salaries & wages
ACC.G10.T2.SALARIES.A1.description: Calculating and recording salary and wage scales and payments: normal time, overtime, deductions (PAYE, pension fund, UIF, medical aid, union membership) and employer contributions (pension, UIF, medical aid, skills development levy), posted through the journals to the ledger.
ACC.G10.T2.SALARIES.A1.strand: Term 2 — VAT, salaries & wages, adjustments & final accounts
ACC.G10.T2.SALARIES.A1.recovery_strategy: Deductions come OUT of the employee's gross pay. Contributions are an EXTRA cost paid BY the employer on top of gross pay.

questions.question: An amount subtracted from an employee's gross pay is a…
questions.memo: Deductions are taken off gross pay.

questions.question: PAYE stands for…
questions.memo: PAYE is employees' tax deducted from pay.

questions.question: UIF stands for…
questions.memo: UIF provides cover when workers lose their jobs.

questions.question: Gross pay minus deductions equals ______ pay.
questions.memo: Net pay is what the employee takes home.

questions.question: Overtime is usually paid at a higher rate than normal time.
questions.memo: Overtime is typically 1.5× or 2× the normal rate.

questions.question: An extra amount the employer pays on top of an employee's wages is a…
questions.memo: Employer contributions add to the cost of employment.

questions.question: Sort each item as a deduction or an employer contribution.
questions.memo: Deductions come off the employee's pay; contributions are an extra employer cost.

questions.question: An employee works 40 normal hours at R50 and 5 overtime hours at R75. The gross wage is…
Gross pay is R10 000 and total deductions are R2 500. Net pay is…
The business pays the PAYE owed to SARS by EFT.
questions.memo: Paying PAYE over: SARS (PAYE) liability (debit) decreases; Bank (credit) decreases.

questions.question: The Skills Development Levy is paid by the…
questions.memo: The SDL is an employer cost.

questions.question: The amount an employee actually takes home is the ______ pay.
questions.memo: Take-home pay is net pay.

questions.question: Which is NOT a deduction from an employee's salary?
questions.memo: The SDL is an employer cost, not an employee deduction.

questions.question: For the employer, a medical aid contribution it pays for staff is…
options: A deduction from its own tax
questions.memo: Employer contributions are an expense.

questions.question: Sort each amount by who ultimately bears it.
questions.memo: Deductions reduce the employee's pay; contributions are extra employer costs.

questions.question: PAYE deducted from employees is paid over to SARS by the employer.
questions.memo: The employer withholds PAYE and remits it to SARS.

questions.question: The total cost of employing a worker is the gross salary plus…
questions.memo: Total cost = gross pay + employer contributions.

questions.question: An employer who deducts PAYE from staff but does not pay it to SARS is acting…
questions.memo: Withholding employees' tax is unethical and illegal.

questions.question: Employer contributions to UIF and pension are recorded as…
questions.memo: Contributions add to the business's expenses.

questions.question: Why does an employer keep a salaries/wages journal?
options: To calculate and record pay, deductions and contributions accurately
questions.expected: To calculate and record pay, deductions and contributions accurately
questions.memo: It ensures accurate, controlled payroll records.

ACC.G10.T2.ADJUSTMENTS.A1.title: Year-end adjustments (sole trader)
ACC.G10.T2.ADJUSTMENTS.A1.description: Year-end adjustments: trading stock deficit/surplus, consumable stores on hand, depreciation (cost/straight-line and diminishing balance), bad debts and bad debts recovered, correction of errors, accrued income, income received in advance, prepaid and accrued expenses, and interest on a mortgage bond.
ACC.G10.T2.ADJUSTMENTS.A1.strand: Term 2 — VAT, salaries & wages, adjustments & final accounts
ACC.G10.T2.ADJUSTMENTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Accrued = owing/earned but not yet paid/received. Prepaid/received-in-advance = paid/received but not yet used/earned. Match each to the correct period.

questions.question: Depreciation is…
options: The spreading of an asset's cost over its useful life
An increase in an asset's value
questions.expected: The spreading of an asset's cost over its useful life
questions.memo: Depreciation allocates cost to the periods that use the asset.

questions.question: An expense owing but not yet paid at year-end is…
questions.memo: Accrued expenses are owing at year-end.

questions.question: An expense paid in advance for next year is…
questions.memo: Prepaid expenses are paid before the period they cover.

questions.question: Income earned but not yet received at year-end is ______ income.
questions.memo: Accrued income is earned but still receivable.

questions.question: A trading stock deficit means there is less stock on hand than the records show.
questions.memo: A deficit is a shortage versus the recorded amount.

questions.question: Consumable stores still on hand at year-end are treated as…
questions.memo: Unused consumables are an asset at year-end.

questions.question: Depreciation is written off on equipment at year-end.
questions.memo: The asset's carrying value falls; depreciation is an expense reducing equity.

questions.question: A trading stock deficit is found at year-end.
questions.memo: Stock (asset) falls; the loss reduces owner's equity.

questions.question: Record telephone expense still owing (accrued) at year-end.
questions.memo: The extra expense reduces equity; the amount owing is a liability.

questions.question: Adjust for rent income received in advance at year-end.
questions.memo: Income earned is reduced now (equity down) and the amount owed to the tenant is a liability.

questions.question: Adjust for insurance prepaid (part belongs to next year).
questions.memo: A prepaid asset is created and the expense is reduced, increasing equity.

questions.question: Record commission income earned but not yet received (accrued income).
questions.memo: Accrued income is an asset; the income increases equity.

questions.question: Writing off an additional bad debt at year-end will…
questions.memo: The debtor falls and the expense reduces profit.

questions.question: Sort each adjustment by whether it creates an asset or a liability at year-end.
questions.memo: Prepaid expenses and accrued income are assets; accrued expenses and income in advance are liabilities.

questions.question: Stock that is short compared with the records is a trading stock ______.
questions.memo: A shortage is a deficit; an excess is a surplus.

questions.question: Depreciation on the diminishing-balance method is calculated on the…
questions.memo: Diminishing balance uses the reducing book value.

questions.question: Depreciation on the cost (straight-line) method is calculated on the…
questions.memo: Straight-line uses the original cost each year.

questions.question: Bad debts recovered (a previously written-off debt now paid) is treated as…
questions.memo: Recovering a written-off debt is income.

questions.question: Record consumable stores still on hand at year-end (the adjustment).
questions.memo: An asset is created for the unused stores and the expense is reduced, raising equity.

questions.question: Why are year-end adjustments necessary?
options: To match income and expenses to the correct period
To reduce the number of debtors
questions.expected: To match income and expenses to the correct period
questions.memo: Adjustments apply the matching principle.

ACC.G10.T2.FINALACCOUNTS.A1.title: Final accounts & Trial Balances
ACC.G10.T2.FINALACCOUNTS.A1.description: The pre-adjustment Trial Balance, closing transfers, the Trading Account and Profit and Loss Account, the post-adjustment and post-closing Trial Balances, and the reversal of certain adjustments at the start of the next period.
ACC.G10.T2.FINALACCOUNTS.A1.strand: Term 2 — VAT, salaries & wages, adjustments & final accounts
ACC.G10.T2.FINALACCOUNTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Only nominal (income/expense) accounts close off to Trading or Profit and Loss. Balance-sheet accounts carry their balance forward.

questions.question: The account used to calculate gross profit is the…
questions.memo: Gross profit is found in the Trading Account.

questions.question: The account used to calculate net profit is the…
questions.memo: Net profit is found in the Profit and Loss Account.

questions.question: Gross profit = sales − cost of ______.
questions.memo: Gross profit = sales − cost of sales.

questions.question: Only nominal (income and expense) accounts are closed off at year-end.
questions.memo: Balance-sheet accounts carry forward; nominal accounts are closed.

questions.question: After the closing entries, the net profit is transferred to…
questions.memo: Net profit increases the owner's capital.

questions.question: Which is the correct order?
options: Pre-adjustment TB → adjustments → post-adjustment TB → closing transfers → post-closing TB
Post-closing TB → closing transfers → adjustments → pre-adjustment TB
Adjustments → pre-adjustment TB → post-closing TB → closing transfers
Closing transfers → adjustments → pre-adjustment TB → post-closing TB
questions.expected: Pre-adjustment TB → adjustments → post-adjustment TB → closing transfers → post-closing TB
questions.memo: The trial balances bracket the adjustments and closing.

questions.question: Sales are R200 000 and cost of sales is R120 000. Gross profit is…
Gross profit R80 000, other income R5 000, expenses R40 000. Net profit is…
Close off the Sales account to the Trading Account.
questions.memo: Closing sales: Sales (debit), Trading account (credit).

questions.question: Close off the Cost of sales account to the Trading Account.
questions.memo: Closing cost of sales: Trading account (debit), Cost of sales (credit).

questions.question: A post-closing Trial Balance contains only…
questions.memo: Nominal accounts are already closed, leaving balance-sheet accounts.

questions.question: Gross profit is transferred from the Trading Account to the ______ Account.
questions.memo: Gross profit moves to the Profit and Loss Account.

questions.question: Which account would NOT appear in the post-closing Trial Balance?
questions.memo: Sales is a nominal account already closed off.

questions.question: Transfer the net profit to the owner's Capital account.
questions.memo: Transferring profit: Profit and Loss (debit), Capital (credit).

questions.question: Accrued expenses are reversed at the start of the new financial period.
questions.memo: Certain adjustments (accruals, prepayments, income in advance) are reversed.

questions.question: Why prepare a post-adjustment Trial Balance?
options: To check the books still balance after the adjustments
questions.expected: To check the books still balance after the adjustments
questions.memo: It confirms debits still equal credits after adjusting.

questions.question: Reversing 'income received in advance' at the start of next year will…
options: Increase income in the new period
Decrease income in the new period
questions.expected: Increase income in the new period
questions.memo: The reversal brings the deferred income into the new year.

questions.question: Which is completed first?
options: The Trading Account, before the Profit and Loss Account
The Profit and Loss Account, before the Trading Account
The Capital Account, before the Trading Account
The Balance Sheet, before the Trading Account
questions.expected: The Trading Account, before the Profit and Loss Account
questions.memo: Gross profit (Trading) feeds the Profit and Loss Account.

questions.question: Closing transfers move the balances of nominal accounts to…
options: The final accounts (Trading and Profit and Loss)
questions.expected: The final accounts (Trading and Profit and Loss)
questions.memo: Nominal balances close to the final accounts.

questions.question: A net loss for the year will…
questions.memo: A loss reduces owner's equity.

ACC.G10.T3.INCOMESTATEMENT.A1.title: Income Statement (sole trader)
ACC.G10.T3.INCOMESTATEMENT.A1.description: Preparing the Income Statement (Statement of Comprehensive Income) of a sole trader from the adjusted figures, with the supporting notes.
ACC.G10.T3.INCOMESTATEMENT.A1.recovery_strategy: The Income Statement shows only income and expenses for the year. Assets, liabilities and equity belong on the Balance Sheet.

questions.question: The Income Statement shows the business's…
options: Profit or loss for a period
questions.expected: Profit or loss for a period
questions.memo: It reports performance over a period.

questions.question: Another name for the Income Statement is the…
questions.memo: The IFRS name is the Statement of Comprehensive Income.

questions.question: Sales − cost of sales = ______ profit.
questions.memo: This difference is gross profit.

questions.question: The Income Statement covers a period of time, not a single date.
questions.memo: It reports over a financial period.

questions.question: Gross profit, less operating expenses, plus other operating income gives…
questions.memo: Operating profit is after operating items.

questions.question: Sort each item by where it belongs.
questions.memo: Income and expenses go to the Income Statement; assets, liabilities and equity to the Balance Sheet.

questions.question: Sales R500 000 and cost of sales R300 000. Gross profit is…
Which is an operating expense?
questions.memo: Salaries are an operating expense.

questions.question: Which is NOT shown in the Income Statement?
questions.memo: A loan is a Balance Sheet liability.

questions.question: Cost of sales is subtracted from sales to get ______ profit.
questions.memo: Sales − cost of sales = gross profit.

questions.question: Which is the correct order in the Income Statement?
options: Sales → Cost of sales → Gross profit → Operating expenses → Operating profit
Operating profit → Sales → Gross profit → Cost of sales
Gross profit → Sales → Operating profit → Cost of sales
Cost of sales → Operating profit → Sales → Gross profit
questions.expected: Sales → Cost of sales → Gross profit → Operating expenses → Operating profit
questions.memo: The statement flows from sales down to operating profit.

questions.question: Depreciation appears in the Income Statement as a/an…
questions.memo: Depreciation is an operating expense.

questions.question: Discount allowed is shown in the Income Statement as a/an…
questions.memo: Discount allowed is an expense.

questions.question: Interest on a loan is shown in the Income Statement as a…
questions.memo: Loan interest is a finance cost.

questions.question: Sort each into operating income or operating expense.
questions.memo: Operating income is earned; operating expenses are running costs.

questions.question: Operating profit R120 000, interest income R3 000, interest expense R10 000. Net profit is…
Cost of sales is treated as an expense in the Income Statement.
questions.memo: Cost of sales is deducted from sales as an expense.

questions.question: If expenses rise while sales stay the same, net profit will…
questions.memo: Higher expenses reduce net profit.

questions.question: The 'Sales' figure in the Income Statement is shown…
options: After deducting goods returned by customers
questions.expected: After deducting goods returned by customers
questions.memo: Net sales exclude debtors' allowances (returns).

questions.question: Why does a sole trader prepare an Income Statement?
options: To measure the profit or loss earned during the year
questions.expected: To measure the profit or loss earned during the year
questions.memo: It reports the year's financial performance.

ACC.G10.T3.BALANCESHEET.A1.title: Balance Sheet & notes (sole trader)
ACC.G10.T3.BALANCESHEET.A1.description: Preparing the Balance Sheet (Statement of Financial Position) of a sole trader and its notes from the adjusted figures.
ACC.G10.T3.BALANCESHEET.A1.recovery_strategy: Assets = Owner's equity + Liabilities, always. Use the notes (fixed assets, trade & other receivables, etc.) to build each total.

questions.question: The Balance Sheet shows the business's…
options: Financial position on a specific date
questions.expected: Financial position on a specific date
questions.memo: It is a snapshot at a date.

questions.question: Another name for the Balance Sheet is the…
questions.memo: The IFRS name is the Statement of Financial Position.

questions.question: Assets = owner's equity + ______.
questions.memo: This is the accounting equation.

questions.question: The Balance Sheet is prepared at a single date, e.g. 28 February.
questions.memo: It reports the position on one date.

questions.question: Vehicles and equipment are examples of…
questions.memo: They are long-term, non-current assets.

questions.question: Sort each item into the correct Balance Sheet group.
questions.memo: Long-term assets are non-current; stock/debtors/bank are current; creditors are a current liability.

questions.question: Which is a current asset?
questions.memo: Stock is a current asset.

questions.question: A loan repayable over five years is a…
questions.memo: Long-term debt is a non-current liability.

questions.question: Creditors (amounts owed to suppliers) are a…
questions.memo: Trade creditors are a current liability.

questions.question: Owner's equity = capital + net profit − ______.
questions.memo: Drawings reduce owner's equity.

questions.question: Which is the correct order on the assets side?
options: Non-current assets → Current assets → Total assets
Total assets → Current assets → Non-current assets
Current assets → Total assets → Non-current assets
Non-current assets → Total assets → Current assets
questions.expected: Non-current assets → Current assets → Total assets
questions.memo: Non-current assets are listed before current assets.

questions.question: Capital at start R100 000, net profit R45 000, drawings R20 000. Closing capital is…
Which is NOT shown on the Balance Sheet?
questions.memo: Sales is an Income Statement item.

questions.question: The Balance Sheet must balance: total assets = owner's equity + liabilities.
questions.memo: It always balances by the accounting equation.

questions.question: Sort each asset as current or non-current.
questions.memo: Current assets are used up within a year; non-current assets are kept longer.

questions.question: Total assets R300 000 and total liabilities R110 000. Owner's equity is…
questions.memo: Equity = assets − liabilities = R300 000 − R110 000 = R190 000.

questions.question: A bank overdraft is shown as a…
questions.memo: An overdraft is a short-term liability.

questions.question: If drawings increase, the owner's equity will…
questions.memo: More drawings reduce equity.

questions.question: Amounts owed by customers (debtors) are shown as a ______ asset.
questions.memo: Debtors are a current asset.

questions.question: Why prepare a Balance Sheet?
options: To show what the business owns and owes at a point in time
questions.expected: To show what the business owns and owes at a point in time
questions.memo: It reports financial position.

ACC.G10.T3.INTERPRET.A1.title: Analysis & interpretation of financial statements
ACC.G10.T3.INTERPRET.A1.description: Calculating and interpreting financial indicators: gross profit on sales, gross profit on cost of sales, net profit on sales, operating expenses on sales, operating profit on sales, current ratio, acid-test ratio, solvency ratio and return on equity.
ACC.G10.T3.INTERPRET.A1.recovery_strategy: Liquidity ratios (current, acid-test) should comfortably cover what is owed; profitability percentages should hold or rise. Compare to last year and to a benchmark.

questions.question: The current ratio measures a business's ability to…
questions.memo: It compares current assets to current liabilities.

questions.question: Return on equity measures…
options: The return the owner earns on their investment
questions.expected: The return the owner earns on their investment
questions.memo: ROE relates profit to owner's equity.

questions.question: Gross profit ÷ sales × 100 gives the gross profit percentage on ______.
questions.memo: This is GP% on sales.

questions.question: A current ratio of 2:1 means current assets are twice current liabilities.
questions.memo: 2:1 means assets are double the liabilities.

questions.question: Current assets R80 000 and current liabilities R40 000. The current ratio is…
The acid-test (quick) ratio excludes which current asset?
questions.memo: Stock is excluded as it is least liquid.

questions.question: Gross profit R60 000 and sales R200 000. The gross profit % on sales is…
Net profit R40 000 and sales R200 000. The net profit % on sales is…
The solvency ratio compares total assets to…
questions.memo: Solvency = total assets : total liabilities.

questions.question: A current ratio that is too low may mean the business cannot pay its ______ debts.
questions.memo: A weak current ratio signals liquidity strain.

questions.question: Compare the liquidity of two businesses.

statements.text: Can comfortably pay its short-term debts
May struggle to pay its short-term debts
Has a current ratio that can be calculated

questions.memo: Source A is liquid; Source B's ratios are too low to cover its debts.

questions.question: Operating expenses R50 000 and sales R200 000. The operating expenses % on sales is…
A higher return on equity is generally better for the owner.
questions.memo: More return per rand invested is better.

questions.question: If the gross profit percentage falls, a possible reason is…
options: Higher cost of sales or lower selling prices
questions.expected: Higher cost of sales or lower selling prices
questions.memo: Margins shrink when costs rise or prices drop.

questions.question: An acid-test ratio of 0.5:1 suggests the business…
options: May struggle to pay debts without selling stock
questions.expected: May struggle to pay debts without selling stock
questions.memo: Below 1:1 means quick assets do not cover current liabilities.

questions.question: Gross profit R60 000 and cost of sales R120 000. The gross profit % on cost of sales is…
Solvency means total assets exceed total liabilities.
questions.memo: A solvent business owns more than it owes.

questions.question: A business with a high current ratio but a low acid-test ratio probably has…
questions.memo: The gap between the ratios is mostly inventory.

questions.question: Why interpret financial statements?
options: To judge performance and make better decisions
questions.expected: To judge performance and make better decisions
questions.memo: Interpretation turns figures into insight.

questions.question: Return on equity = net profit ÷ ______ × 100.
questions.memo: ROE relates profit to the owner's equity.

ACC.G10.T4.COSTCONCEPTS.A1.title: Cost accounting concepts (manufacturing)
ACC.G10.T4.COSTCONCEPTS.A1.description: Basic cost concepts of a manufacturing business: direct and indirect labour, direct (raw) and indirect materials, factory overhead costs, prime cost, variable costs, fixed costs and work-in-process.
ACC.G10.T4.COSTCONCEPTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Direct costs can be traced straight to the product (raw materials, machine operators). Indirect costs (factory rent, cleaning) support production but are not in the product itself.

questions.question: Direct materials are also called…
questions.memo: Direct materials are the raw materials in the product.

questions.question: The wages of machine operators who make the product are…
questions.memo: Operators' wages are direct labour.

questions.question: Direct materials + direct labour = ______ cost.
questions.memo: Prime cost is direct materials plus direct labour.

questions.question: Factory rent is a factory overhead cost.
questions.memo: Factory rent is an indirect (overhead) cost.

questions.question: Costs that stay the same in total regardless of output are…
questions.memo: Fixed costs do not change with output.

questions.question: Costs that change in total as output changes are…
questions.memo: Variable costs rise and fall with output.

questions.question: Sort each cost as direct or indirect.
questions.memo: Direct costs trace to the product; indirect costs support production.

questions.question: Sort each cost as fixed or variable.
questions.memo: Fixed costs stay constant in total; variable costs change with output.

questions.question: Glue and screws used generally around the factory are…
questions.memo: Small shared materials are indirect materials.

questions.question: Prime cost is made up of…
questions.memo: Prime cost = direct materials + direct labour.

questions.question: Partly finished goods at year-end are called work-in-______.
questions.memo: Unfinished goods are work-in-process.

questions.question: The factory supervisor's salary is classified as…
questions.memo: Supervision is indirect labour, an overhead.

questions.question: Direct costs can be traced directly to the product made.
questions.memo: That traceability is what makes them 'direct'.

questions.question: Which is a variable cost?
questions.memo: Material usage changes with output.

questions.question: Sort each cost into its category.
questions.memo: Materials in the product, labour making it, and other factory costs.

questions.question: If output doubles, total variable cost will…
questions.memo: Variable cost moves in proportion to output.

questions.question: If output doubles, the fixed cost per unit will…
questions.memo: Fixed cost spread over more units falls per unit.

questions.question: Factory overheads include…
options: Indirect materials, indirect labour and other factory running costs
questions.expected: Indirect materials, indirect labour and other factory running costs
questions.memo: Overheads are the indirect factory costs.

questions.question: Administration and selling costs are part of factory overheads.
questions.memo: They are non-manufacturing costs, not factory overheads.

questions.question: Why classify costs as direct or indirect?
options: To work out the true cost of making the product
To reduce the number of staff
questions.expected: To work out the true cost of making the product
questions.memo: Cost classification supports accurate product costing.

ACC.G10.T4.BUDGETCONCEPTS.A1.title: Budgeting concepts
ACC.G10.T4.BUDGETCONCEPTS.A1.description: Basic budgeting concepts: the cash budget, zero-based budget, capital budget, long-term budget and medium-term budget.
ACC.G10.T4.BUDGETCONCEPTS.A1.recovery_strategy: A cash budget only tracks money actually flowing in and out. Non-cash items like depreciation never appear in it.

questions.question: A budget is…
options: A financial plan for the future
questions.expected: A financial plan for the future
questions.memo: A budget plans future finances.

questions.question: A cash budget plans the business's expected…
questions.memo: A cash budget plans cash in and out.

questions.question: A budget prepared from zero each time, justifying every item, is a ______-based budget.
questions.memo: Zero-based budgeting justifies every item afresh.

questions.question: A budget helps a business plan and control its money.
questions.memo: Planning and control are the main reasons to budget.

questions.question: A budget for buying fixed assets is a…
questions.memo: Capital budgets plan major asset purchases.

questions.question: A budget covering more than one year is a…
questions.memo: Long-term budgets span several years.

questions.question: Match each budget to its description.
questions.memo: Each budget type has a distinct purpose.

questions.question: Which item would NOT appear in a cash budget?
questions.memo: Depreciation is non-cash, so it is excluded.

questions.question: A cash budget includes only actual cash flowing in and out.
questions.memo: Only real cash movements appear.

questions.question: Comparing the budget to the actual figures helps a business…
questions.memo: Budget-to-actual comparison is a control tool.

questions.question: A budget covering a few months up to a year is a ______-term budget.
questions.memo: Medium-term budgets span months up to a year.

questions.question: A medium-term budget typically covers…
options: A period of months up to about a year
questions.expected: A period of months up to about a year
questions.memo: Medium-term is months to a year.

questions.question: Why prepare a cash budget?
options: To make sure there is enough cash when needed
questions.expected: To make sure there is enough cash when needed
questions.memo: It anticipates cash shortages and surpluses.

questions.question: Sort each item by whether it appears in a cash budget.
questions.memo: Only actual cash flows appear; non-cash items do not.

questions.question: A capital budget plans large purchases like vehicles and machinery.
questions.memo: Capital budgets cover major asset spending.

questions.question: If a cash budget shows a future shortfall, the business should…
options: Arrange finance or cut payments in advance
questions.expected: Arrange finance or cut payments in advance
questions.memo: Planning ahead lets it manage the shortfall.

questions.question: Zero-based budgeting differs from normal budgeting because…
options: Every item must be justified from zero, not based on last year
questions.expected: Every item must be justified from zero, not based on last year
questions.memo: Each item starts from a clean slate.

questions.question: A budget that is never compared to the actual results is…
questions.memo: Without comparison, control is lost.

questions.question: Planning for cash helps the business stay ______ (able to pay its debts).
questions.memo: Good cash planning keeps the business liquid.

questions.question: Why do businesses budget?
options: To plan ahead, allocate resources and control spending
questions.expected: To plan ahead, allocate resources and control spending
questions.memo: Budgeting supports planning and control.

ACC.G11.T1.ETHICS.A1.title: Ethics in the financial environment
ACC.G11.T1.ETHICS.A1.description: Identifying and analysing ethical behaviour in financial environments with reference to accountability, transparency and sustainability, integrated through appropriate scenarios.
ACC.G11.T1.ETHICS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Ethics, audit, reconciliations, fixed assets & partnerships
ACC.G11.T1.ETHICS.A1.recovery_strategy: Judge against accountability, transparency and sustainability. If an action hides information, harms stakeholders, or is not sustainable, it is unethical.

questions.question: Accountability in business means…
options: Being answerable for your decisions and actions
questions.expected: Being answerable for your decisions and actions
questions.memo: Accountability means taking responsibility and being answerable.

questions.question: Sustainability considers the impact of the business on future generations.
questions.memo: Sustainability balances present needs with the future.

questions.question: Transparency means financial information is…
questions.memo: Transparency means open, honest disclosure.

questions.question: A factory dumps waste illegally to cut costs. This mainly breaks…
questions.memo: Harming the environment ignores sustainability.

questions.question: Directors hide poor results from shareholders. This breaks…
questions.memo: Hiding results is neither transparent nor accountable.

questions.question: Build a short answer on why accountability matters.
questions.prompt: Why does accountability matter in business?

options.text: Accountability means people answer for their decisions
Accountability means making more sales
Managers must explain how funds were used
The business pays no tax
So resources are used responsibly and trust is built
So losses can be hidden

questions.memo: Accountability links responsibility to trust and good stewardship.

questions.question: Compare two companies' reporting.

source_a.text: Source A: publishes full, true results and discloses risks.

source_b.text: Source B: hides debt and overstates profit.
