questions.memo: Source A is ethical; Source B deceives stakeholders.

questions.question: An accountant who knowingly signs off false figures is…
options: Acting unethically and may face disciplinary action
questions.expected: Acting unethically and may face disciplinary action
questions.memo: Certifying false figures is a serious ethical breach.

questions.question: Ethical businesses consider profit, people and the planet.
questions.memo: The 'triple bottom line' balances all three.

questions.question: Paying suppliers fairly and on time shows…
questions.memo: Fair, timely payment is responsible and ethical.

questions.question: Which is an example of poor sustainability?
options: Using resources wastefully with no plan for the future
questions.expected: Using resources wastefully with no plan for the future
questions.memo: Wasteful use ignores the future.

questions.question: Build a short answer on why transparency builds trust.

options.text: Transparency means stakeholders see the true position
Transparency means hiding bad news
Investors and SARS rely on the disclosed figures
It removes the need for an auditor
So stakeholders can trust and support the business
So the business avoids all expenses

questions.memo: Transparency lets stakeholders trust and back the business.

questions.question: Paying a bribe to win a tender is…
questions.memo: Bribery is corrupt and unethical.

questions.question: Reporting fraud (whistle-blowing) can be an ethical act.
questions.memo: Reporting wrongdoing is ethical and often protected.

questions.question: Compare two responses to a conflict of interest.

source_a.text: Source A: declares the conflict and steps aside from the decision.

source_b.text: Source B: hides the conflict and approves the deal anyway.

questions.memo: Declaring and stepping aside is ethical; hiding it is not.

questions.question: The best long-term reason to act ethically is that it…
options: Builds trust and a sustainable business
questions.expected: Builds trust and a sustainable business
questions.memo: Ethics underpins lasting success.

questions.question: A business that treats its workers fairly and safely is showing…
questions.memo: Fair, safe treatment of staff is socially responsible.

questions.question: Hiding environmental damage from the public breaks…
questions.memo: It conceals harm and ignores the future.

questions.question: Ethics applies to how a business treats employees, customers and the environment.
questions.memo: Ethics covers all stakeholders.

questions.question: Why is sustainability important to a business's future?
options: Its resources and reputation must last for it to survive
It removes the need for profit
questions.expected: Its resources and reputation must last for it to survive
questions.memo: Sustainable use protects future operations and reputation.

ACC.G11.T1.AUDIT.A1.title: Internal audit & control
ACC.G11.T1.AUDIT.A1.description: Internal audit processes: the meaning of an internal audit, the difference between internal control and an internal audit, the role of the internal auditor, division of duties, documentation and physical controls, and audit procedures for cash, credit, stock, debtors and creditors.
ACC.G11.T1.AUDIT.A1.strand: Term 1 — Ethics, audit, reconciliations, fixed assets & partnerships
ACC.G11.T1.AUDIT.A1.recovery_strategy: Internal CONTROL is the day-to-day system that prevents errors/fraud. Internal AUDIT independently checks that the controls are working.

questions.question: An internal audit is…
options: An independent check that the controls are working
questions.expected: An independent check that the controls are working
questions.memo: Internal audit independently reviews the control system.

questions.question: The difference between internal control and internal audit is that…
options: Control is the daily system; audit checks that the system works
Audit records cash; control checks it
questions.expected: Control is the daily system; audit checks that the system works
questions.memo: Control operates daily; audit reviews it.

questions.question: The internal auditor is employed by the business itself.
questions.memo: Internal auditors work within the organisation.

questions.question: Division of duties means…
options: No one person controls a whole transaction
questions.expected: No one person controls a whole transaction
questions.memo: Splitting duties reduces fraud and error.

questions.question: Match each audit procedure to the area it controls.

items.text: Count cash in the till daily

questions.memo: Each procedure safeguards a particular area.

questions.question: Why divide duties between staff?
options: To reduce the chance of fraud and error
questions.expected: To reduce the chance of fraud and error
questions.memo: Separation makes hidden fraud harder.

questions.question: Checking that goods received match the order and invoice is a control over…
questions.memo: It controls the purchasing/creditors cycle.

questions.question: An internal audit can recommend improvements to the controls.
questions.memo: Audit findings drive control improvements.

questions.question: Pre-numbered documents help the auditor because…
options: A missing number reveals a missing transaction
questions.expected: A missing number reveals a missing transaction
questions.memo: Sequential numbering exposes gaps.

questions.question: Physical controls over stock include…
questions.memo: Physical security protects stock.

questions.question: Sort each as a strength or weakness of internal control.
questions.memo: Strengths protect assets; weaknesses leave gaps.

questions.question: An audit trail is…
options: The documentary path that lets a transaction be traced
A walking route in the factory
questions.expected: The documentary path that lets a transaction be traced
questions.memo: The audit trail links documents to records.

questions.question: Internal audit is part of good corporate governance.
questions.memo: Sound governance relies on internal audit.

questions.question: A weak internal audit increases the risk of…
questions.memo: Weak audit lets problems go unnoticed.

questions.question: Reconciling the bank monthly is a control over…
questions.memo: Bank reconciliation controls cash.

questions.question: The internal auditor normally reports to…
questions.memo: Internal audit reports to those charged with governance.

questions.question: Internal and external auditors are exactly the same thing.
questions.memo: Internal auditors work inside; external auditors are independent.

questions.question: The main aim of internal audit is to…
options: Give assurance that controls work and assets are safe
questions.expected: Give assurance that controls work and assets are safe
questions.memo: Audit assures owners the system is sound.

questions.question: Match each procedure to the cycle it checks.
questions.memo: Each control belongs to a specific business cycle.

questions.question: Why is internal audit important to owners?
options: It gives independent assurance their resources are well managed
It removes the need for a ledger
questions.expected: It gives independent assurance their resources are well managed
questions.memo: Owners gain confidence their assets are protected.

ACC.G11.T1.BANKREC.A1.title: Bank reconciliation
ACC.G11.T1.BANKREC.A1.description: Reconciling the bank statement with the cash journals to prepare a bank reconciliation statement: outstanding deposits, cheques not yet presented, stop/debit orders, direct transfers, bank charges, interest, errors and omissions, R/D or cancelled cheques and post-dated cheques.
ACC.G11.T1.BANKREC.A1.strand: Term 1 — Ethics, audit, reconciliations, fixed assets & partnerships
ACC.G11.T1.BANKREC.A1.recovery_strategy: Outstanding deposits are added and unpresented cheques subtracted from the bank statement balance. Bank charges and interest update the cash book.

questions.question: A bank reconciliation compares the cash journals with the…
questions.memo: It reconciles the business's records with the bank's.

questions.question: A deposit recorded by the business but not yet on the bank statement is an ______ deposit.
questions.memo: It is outstanding (not yet reflected by the bank).

questions.question: A cheque issued by the business but not yet paid by the bank is…
questions.memo: It has not yet been presented for payment.

questions.question: Bank charges appear on the bank statement first and must then be entered in the cash book.
questions.memo: The business learns of them from the statement.

questions.question: On the bank reconciliation statement, outstanding deposits are…
options: Added to the bank statement balance
questions.expected: Added to the bank statement balance
questions.memo: Deposits not yet shown are added back.

questions.question: Outstanding (unpresented) cheques are…
options: Subtracted from the bank statement balance
questions.expected: Subtracted from the bank statement balance
questions.memo: Unpresented cheques are deducted.

questions.question: On the bank reconciliation statement, sort each item.

items.text: Deposit not yet credited by bank

questions.memo: Outstanding deposits are added; unpresented cheques are subtracted.

questions.question: Bank charges not yet in the cash book are entered in the…
questions.memo: Charges reduce the bank — CPJ.

questions.question: A debit order on the bank statement but not in the books must be…
options: Entered in the Cash Payments Journal
questions.expected: Entered in the Cash Payments Journal
questions.memo: Debit orders are payments — CPJ.

questions.question: An R/D (returned) cheque reduces the bank ______.
questions.memo: A bounced cheque lowers the bank balance.

questions.question: Which is the correct order to reconcile the bank?
options: Compare cash book to statement → update cash book for new items → list timing differences → prepare reconciliation statement
Prepare reconciliation statement → compare → update cash book → list differences
Update cash book → prepare statement → compare → list differences
List differences → prepare statement → compare → update cash book
questions.expected: Compare cash book to statement → update cash book for new items → list timing differences → prepare reconciliation statement
questions.memo: First update the books, then reconcile the timing differences.

questions.question: Direct deposits by debtors shown on the statement are entered in the…
questions.memo: Direct deposits increase the bank — CRJ.

questions.question: Interest received from the bank is entered in the Cash Receipts Journal.
questions.memo: Interest received increases the bank — CRJ.

questions.question: The aim of a bank reconciliation is to…
options: Explain the difference between the cash book and the bank statement
questions.expected: Explain the difference between the cash book and the bank statement
questions.memo: It reconciles the two records.

questions.question: Sort each item by which record must be updated.
questions.memo: Items the bank knows but the books don't update the cash book; timing items go on the statement.

questions.question: A favourable bank balance in the business's cash book appears on the bank statement as a…
options: Credit balance (from the bank's point of view)
questions.expected: Credit balance (from the bank's point of view)
questions.memo: The bank owes the customer, so it is a credit on the statement.

questions.question: A stale or cancelled cheque should be…
options: Cancelled and the bank increased again
questions.expected: Cancelled and the bank increased again
questions.memo: Cancelling the cheque restores the bank balance.

questions.question: After reconciliation, the adjusted cash book balance should agree with the reconciliation statement.
questions.memo: Reconciliation makes the two agree.

questions.question: Why reconcile the bank every month?
options: To detect errors, omissions and possible fraud
questions.expected: To detect errors, omissions and possible fraud
questions.memo: Regular reconciliation is a key cash control.

questions.question: Post-dated cheques received should not yet be entered as ______.
questions.memo: A post-dated cheque cannot be banked yet, so it is not yet a receipt.

ACC.G11.T1.CREDITORSREC.A1.title: Creditors reconciliation
ACC.G11.T1.CREDITORSREC.A1.description: Reconciling statements received from creditors with the accounts in the Creditors' Ledger to prepare creditors' reconciliation statements: outstanding invoices or credit notes, outstanding payments, discounts not recorded, and the correction of errors or omissions.
ACC.G11.T1.CREDITORSREC.A1.strand: Term 1 — Ethics, audit, reconciliations, fixed assets & partnerships
ACC.G11.T1.CREDITORSREC.A1.recovery_strategy: Find the difference, decide which record is wrong, and correct that one. The reconciled creditor's account must agree with the supplier's statement.

questions.question: A creditors reconciliation compares the supplier's statement with the…
options: Creditor's account in the Creditors' Ledger
questions.expected: Creditor's account in the Creditors' Ledger
questions.memo: It reconciles our ledger with the supplier's statement.

questions.question: An invoice on the supplier's statement but not yet in our books is an ______ invoice.
questions.memo: It is outstanding in our records.

questions.question: A creditors reconciliation helps confirm the amount owed to a supplier.
questions.memo: It checks our balance against the supplier's.

questions.question: A payment we made but not yet on the supplier's statement should be…
questions.memo: Our payment reduces what the statement still shows owing.

questions.question: A discount we recorded but the supplier did not is…
options: A difference to investigate and resolve
questions.expected: A difference to investigate and resolve
questions.memo: Differences must be traced and corrected.

questions.question: Sort each difference by which record to act on.

items.text: Our payment not yet on their statement
A cheque we sent is in transit

questions.memo: Our errors fix our ledger; timing differences are shown on the reconciliation.

questions.question: The purpose of a creditors reconciliation is to…
options: Ensure our records agree with the supplier's
questions.expected: Ensure our records agree with the supplier's
questions.memo: It aligns the two records before payment.

questions.question: If our ledger shows R5 000 but the statement shows R5 800, there is a ______ to find.
questions.memo: An R800 difference must be located and explained.

questions.question: If we omitted a supplier invoice, our balance is…
questions.memo: A missing invoice understates what we owe.

questions.question: Reconciling creditors reduces the risk of overpaying a supplier.
questions.memo: It ensures we pay only what we truly owe.

questions.question: A credit note from a supplier, not yet recorded, will…
questions.memo: A credit note reduces our liability.

questions.question: Match each difference to its likely cause.

items.text: Cheque not yet received by supplier

questions.memo: Timing differences resolve themselves; errors must be corrected.

questions.question: Why is reconciling creditors part of internal control?
options: It prevents paying incorrect amounts and detects errors or fraud
questions.expected: It prevents paying incorrect amounts and detects errors or fraud
questions.memo: It protects cash and ensures accuracy.

questions.question: If the supplier charged us for goods we returned, we should…
options: Query it and not pay for the returns
questions.expected: Query it and not pay for the returns
questions.memo: Returned goods should be credited, not paid for.

questions.question: Outstanding payments are deducted from the ______ statement balance.
questions.memo: Our unrecorded-by-them payments reduce the supplier's balance.

questions.question: Discounts not recorded by either party can cause a reconciling difference.
questions.memo: Unrecorded discounts create differences to resolve.

questions.question: Reconciling before paying a supplier helps the business…
options: Pay only what it truly owes
questions.expected: Pay only what it truly owes
questions.memo: It prevents over- or under-payment.

questions.question: A supplier statement is the document sent by the…
questions.memo: Suppliers send statements of what we owe them.

questions.question: A creditors reconciliation is done for each individual creditor.
questions.memo: Each supplier account is reconciled separately.

questions.question: The main benefit of creditors reconciliation is…
options: Accurate amounts owed and good supplier relations
questions.expected: Accurate amounts owed and good supplier relations
questions.memo: Accuracy and trust with suppliers are the key benefits.

ACC.G11.T1.FIXEDASSETS.A1.title: Fixed/tangible assets
ACC.G11.T1.FIXEDASSETS.A1.description: The fixed/tangible asset register, recording the acquisition of assets, calculating and recording depreciation (straight-line and diminishing balance), how fully depreciated assets are shown, and recording the disposal of assets (cash, credit, trade-in) at the start, during and end of a financial year.
ACC.G11.T1.FIXEDASSETS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Ethics, audit, reconciliations, fixed assets & partnerships
ACC.G11.T1.FIXEDASSETS.A1.recovery_strategy: When disposing of an asset, first record depreciation up to the disposal date, then transfer cost and accumulated depreciation to the Asset Disposal account.

questions.question: Depreciation is recorded in order to…
options: Spread the asset's cost over its useful life
questions.expected: Spread the asset's cost over its useful life
questions.memo: Depreciation allocates cost over time.

questions.question: The fixed asset register keeps a record of…
options: Each asset, its cost and its depreciation
questions.expected: Each asset, its cost and its depreciation
questions.memo: It tracks each asset for control.

questions.question: Cost minus accumulated depreciation = ______ value.
questions.memo: Carrying (book) value = cost − accumulated depreciation.

questions.question: Straight-line depreciation is the same amount each year.
questions.memo: Straight-line spreads cost evenly.

questions.question: Diminishing-balance depreciation is calculated on the…
questions.memo: Diminishing balance uses the reducing carrying value.

questions.question: Record the depreciation for the year.
questions.memo: Depreciation (debit, expense); Accumulated depreciation (credit).

questions.question: The business buys a vehicle and pays cash.
questions.memo: Vehicle for cash: Vehicles (debit), Bank (credit).

questions.question: The business buys equipment on credit.
questions.memo: Equipment on credit: Equipment (debit), Creditors control (credit).

questions.question: Cost R100 000 and accumulated depreciation R40 000. The carrying value is…
Straight-line depreciation on a cost of R80 000 at 20% per year is…
Which is the correct order when disposing of an asset?
options: Record depreciation to date → transfer cost and accumulated depreciation to disposal → record proceeds → calculate profit/loss
Record proceeds → calculate profit/loss → record depreciation → transfer cost
Calculate profit/loss → record proceeds → transfer cost → record depreciation
Transfer cost → record proceeds → record depreciation → calculate profit/loss
questions.expected: Record depreciation to date → transfer cost and accumulated depreciation to disposal → record proceeds → calculate profit/loss
questions.memo: Depreciate to the disposal date first, then work through the disposal account.

questions.question: A profit on the disposal of an asset arises when the proceeds exceed the…
questions.memo: Profit on disposal = proceeds − carrying value.

questions.question: A fully depreciated asset still in use is kept at a carrying value of R______.
questions.memo: Once fully depreciated, its carrying value is nil (or R1 for record-keeping).

questions.question: Cash is received on the disposal of an old asset.
questions.memo: Proceeds on disposal: Bank (debit), Asset disposal (credit).

questions.question: Depreciation must be recorded up to the date an asset is disposed of.
questions.memo: Depreciation is brought up to date before disposal.

questions.question: The diminishing-balance method gives higher depreciation in…
questions.memo: It charges more early on as the carrying value is higher.

questions.question: A loss on disposal occurs when the proceeds are…
questions.memo: Proceeds below carrying value give a loss.

questions.question: Why keep a fixed asset register?
options: For control and accurate depreciation records
questions.expected: For control and accurate depreciation records
questions.memo: It supports control and correct depreciation.

questions.question: A new delivery vehicle is bought entirely on credit.
questions.memo: Vehicle on credit: Vehicles (debit), Creditors control (credit).

questions.question: Looking after the business's fixed assets responsibly is an example of…
options: Responsible management and good internal control
questions.expected: Responsible management and good internal control
questions.memo: Caring for assets is responsible and controlled.

ACC.G11.T1.PARTCONCEPTS.A1.title: Partnerships: concepts & GAAP
ACC.G11.T1.PARTCONCEPTS.A1.description: Concepts unique to partnerships — partnership, capital accounts, current accounts, interest on capital, salaries and bonus to partners, division of profits/losses — together with the GAAP principles applied to partnerships.
ACC.G11.T1.PARTCONCEPTS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Ethics, audit, reconciliations, fixed assets & partnerships
ACC.G11.T1.PARTCONCEPTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Capital accounts hold the fixed contributions. Current accounts hold the year's profit share, salaries, interest on capital and drawings.

questions.question: A partnership is a business owned by…
questions.memo: Partnerships have two or more owners.

questions.question: Each partner's fixed contribution is recorded in the…
questions.memo: Fixed contributions sit in the capital account.

questions.question: A partner's share of profit, salary and drawings is recorded in the…
questions.memo: Year-to-year movements go through the current account.

questions.question: Interest on ______ rewards partners for the money they have invested.
questions.memo: Interest on capital rewards the partners' investment.

questions.question: Partners can be paid a salary as part of sharing the profit.
questions.memo: Partner salaries are an appropriation of profit.

questions.question: A bonus to a partner is…
options: An additional share of profit for extra responsibility
questions.expected: An additional share of profit for extra responsibility
questions.memo: A bonus rewards extra contribution.

questions.question: Sort each item into the correct partner account.
questions.memo: Fixed contributions are capital; profit share, salaries, interest and drawings are current.

questions.question: Profits are divided between partners according to…
questions.memo: The agreement sets the profit-sharing ratio.

questions.question: If there is no agreement, profits are shared…
questions.memo: Without an agreement, profits are shared equally.

questions.question: The document setting out how partners share profits is the partnership ______.
questions.memo: The partnership agreement governs profit sharing.

questions.question: A partnership has unlimited liability for its debts.
questions.memo: Partners are personally liable for partnership debts.

questions.question: Interest on capital is calculated on each partner's…
questions.memo: It is based on the capital invested.

questions.question: Drawings by a partner…
questions.memo: Drawings reduce the current account.

questions.question: Sort each item as an appropriation of profit or a normal expense.
questions.memo: Partner rewards are appropriations; running costs are expenses.

questions.question: Why apply GAAP to partnership accounts?
questions.memo: GAAP keeps the statements consistent and trustworthy.

questions.question: Partners A and B share profits 3:2. Profit is R50 000 (no salaries or interest). A's share is…
Each partner's capital account normally has a credit balance.
questions.memo: Capital (equity) is a credit balance.

questions.question: A current account with a debit balance means the partner has…
options: Drawn more than their share of profit
questions.expected: Drawn more than their share of profit
questions.memo: Excess drawings create a debit current balance.

questions.question: Salaries and interest to partners are an ______ of profit, not an expense.
questions.memo: They share out profit rather than reduce it as an expense.

questions.question: An advantage of a partnership over a sole trader is…
questions.memo: Partners pool capital and skills.

ACC.G11.T1.PARTLEDGER.A1.title: Partnerships: ledger, adjustments & final accounts
ACC.G11.T1.PARTLEDGER.A1.description: The partnership accounting cycle, year-end adjustments (including provision for bad debts, salaries and bonus to partners, interest on capital and interest on loan), and the Trading, Profit and Loss and Appropriation accounts.
ACC.G11.T1.PARTLEDGER.A1.strand: Term 1 — Ethics, audit, reconciliations, fixed assets & partnerships
ACC.G11.T1.PARTLEDGER.A1.recovery_strategy: After the Profit and Loss Account gives net profit, the Appropriation Account shares it: partner salaries, interest on capital, then the remaining profit in the agreed ratio.

questions.question: The Appropriation Account divides the…
questions.memo: It shares net profit per the agreement.

questions.question: A provision for bad debts is created to…
options: Allow for debtors who may not pay
questions.expected: Allow for debtors who may not pay
questions.memo: It provides for likely uncollectable debts.

questions.question: Net profit is calculated in the Profit and Loss Account before being shared in the ______ account.
questions.memo: Net profit flows into the Appropriation Account.

questions.question: Record interest on capital owed to Partner A.
questions.memo: Interest on capital: Appropriation (debit), Current account: A (credit).

questions.question: Record the salary owed to Partner B.
questions.memo: Partner salary: Appropriation (debit), Current account: B (credit).

questions.question: The provision for bad debts is increased at year-end.
questions.memo: Net debtors (asset) fall; the increase is an expense reducing equity.

questions.question: Interest on a loan from a partner is accrued (owing) at year-end.
questions.memo: The interest expense reduces equity; the amount owing is a liability.

questions.question: An additional bad debt is written off at year-end.
questions.memo: Debtors (asset) fall; the bad debt is an expense reducing equity.

questions.question: Close the net profit to the Appropriation Account.
questions.memo: Net profit: Profit and Loss (debit), Appropriation (credit).

questions.question: Transfer Partner A's share of the remaining profit.
questions.memo: Profit share: Appropriation (debit), Current account: A (credit).

questions.question: After salaries and interest on capital, the remaining profit is shared in the…
questions.memo: The balance is split in the agreed ratio.

questions.question: A ______ for bad debts reduces the value of debtors shown in the Balance Sheet.
questions.memo: The provision is netted against debtors.

questions.question: Interest on a loan from a partner is treated as…
options: An expense (in the Profit and Loss Account)
questions.expected: An expense (in the Profit and Loss Account)
questions.memo: Loan interest is an expense, unlike interest on capital.

questions.question: Partners' salaries in a partnership are…
questions.memo: Partner salaries appropriate profit.

questions.question: The Appropriation Account starts with the net profit from the Profit and Loss Account.
questions.memo: Net profit is the opening figure of the Appropriation Account.

questions.question: If total appropriations exceed the net profit, partners may end up with…
options: Debit balances on their current accounts
questions.expected: Debit balances on their current accounts
questions.memo: Over-distribution leaves debit current balances.

questions.question: Record cash drawings taken by Partner A during the year.
questions.memo: Drawings: Drawings: A (debit), Bank (credit).

questions.question: Year-end adjustments for a partnership include…
options: Depreciation, accruals, prepayments and provision for bad debts
questions.expected: Depreciation, accruals, prepayments and provision for bad debts
questions.memo: The same adjustments as a sole trader, plus partner items.

questions.question: Consumable stores on hand are recorded at year-end (the adjustment).
questions.memo: An asset is created for unused stores and the expense reduced, raising equity.

questions.question: Why prepare an Appropriation Account?
options: To divide the profit fairly per the partnership agreement
questions.expected: To divide the profit fairly per the partnership agreement
questions.memo: It allocates profit per the agreement.

ACC.G11.T1.PARTSTATEMENTS.A1.title: Partnerships: financial statements & notes
ACC.G11.T1.PARTSTATEMENTS.A1.description: Preparing the Income Statement and Balance Sheet of a partnership and the supporting notes (including the partners' current accounts), and reversing certain adjustments at the start of the next period.
ACC.G11.T1.PARTSTATEMENTS.A1.strand: Term 1 — Ethics, audit, reconciliations, fixed assets & partnerships
ACC.G11.T1.PARTSTATEMENTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Partnership equity = capital accounts + current accounts. The current accounts note shows salaries, interest, profit share and drawings for each partner.

questions.question: Partnership equity is made up of…
questions.memo: Equity = capital + current accounts.

questions.question: The note that shows each partner's salary, interest and profit share is the…
questions.memo: The current accounts note details partner movements.

questions.question: The Balance Sheet of a partnership shows ______ accounts and current accounts under equity.
questions.memo: Equity comprises capital and current accounts.

questions.question: The Income Statement of a partnership is similar to that of a sole trader.
questions.memo: The trading results are prepared the same way.

questions.question: Sort each item by where it appears.
questions.memo: Income and expenses to the Income Statement; equity and assets to the Balance Sheet.

questions.question: Where do partners' salaries appear?
options: In the Appropriation/current accounts note, not as an Income Statement expense
As an operating expense in the Income Statement
questions.expected: In the Appropriation/current accounts note, not as an Income Statement expense
questions.memo: Partner salaries are appropriations, shown in the notes.

questions.question: Which is the correct order?
options: Profit and Loss Account → Appropriation Account → Current accounts note → Balance Sheet
Balance Sheet → Appropriation Account → Profit and Loss Account
Current accounts note → Balance Sheet → Profit and Loss Account
Appropriation Account → Profit and Loss Account → Balance Sheet
questions.expected: Profit and Loss Account → Appropriation Account → Current accounts note → Balance Sheet
questions.memo: Profit is found, appropriated, detailed in the note, then shown on the Balance Sheet.

questions.question: A partner's closing current account = opening balance + salary + interest + profit share − …
questions.memo: Drawings reduce the current account.

questions.question: Accrued expenses are ______ at the start of the next financial period.
questions.memo: Certain adjustments are reversed in the new year.

questions.question: Total equity in the Balance Sheet equals capital accounts plus…
questions.memo: Equity = capital + current accounts.

questions.question: Each partner's current account can have a debit or a credit balance.
questions.memo: It depends on profit share versus drawings.

questions.question: Which appears under non-current assets in the Balance Sheet?
questions.memo: Tangible assets are non-current, at carrying value.

questions.question: Sort each asset as current or non-current.
questions.memo: Current assets are short-term; non-current assets are long-term.

questions.question: If a partner's current account is in debit, it is shown…
options: As a deduction within the equity section
questions.expected: As a deduction within the equity section
questions.memo: A debit current account reduces total equity.

questions.question: Notes to the financial statements are prepared to…
options: Give detail supporting the statement figures
questions.expected: Give detail supporting the statement figures
questions.memo: Notes explain and support the figures.

questions.question: Income received in advance is shown as a ______ liability in the Balance Sheet.
questions.memo: It will be settled within a year, so it is current.

questions.question: Why do partnerships keep current accounts?
options: To keep each partner's profit share and drawings separate from fixed capital
questions.expected: To keep each partner's profit share and drawings separate from fixed capital
questions.memo: Current accounts separate ongoing movements from capital.

questions.question: The Balance Sheet of a partnership must balance.
questions.memo: Assets always equal equity plus liabilities.

questions.question: Drawings during the year are closed off to the partner's…
questions.memo: Drawings close to the current account.

questions.question: The main purpose of partnership financial statements is to…
options: Show the performance and position fairly to the partners
questions.expected: Show the performance and position fairly to the partners
questions.memo: They report performance and position to the partners.

ACC.G11.T2.PARTINTERPRET.A1.title: Partnerships: analysis & interpretation
ACC.G11.T2.PARTINTERPRET.A1.description: Analysing and interpreting partnership financial statements: the Grade 10 indicators plus stock turnover rate, stock holding period, average debtors' collection period, average creditors' payment period, debt-equity ratio (gearing), partners' earnings and return on partners' equity.
ACC.G11.T2.PARTINTERPRET.A1.recovery_strategy: Gearing measures reliance on borrowed funds; high gearing is risky if returns fall. Compare each indicator to last year and to the cost of borrowing.

questions.question: The stock turnover rate measures…
options: How many times stock is sold and replaced in a period
How much cash is in the bank
questions.expected: How many times stock is sold and replaced in a period
questions.memo: Turnover shows how fast stock moves.

questions.question: The debtors' collection period measures…
options: How long, on average, debtors take to pay
questions.expected: How long, on average, debtors take to pay
questions.memo: It shows the average days to collect.

questions.question: A high stock turnover usually means stock is selling ______.
questions.memo: Faster turnover means stock sells quickly.

questions.question: A long debtors' collection period can cause cash flow problems.
questions.memo: Slow collection ties up cash.

questions.question: The debt-equity (gearing) ratio compares…
questions.memo: Gearing measures reliance on debt.

questions.question: Cost of sales R600 000 and average stock R100 000. The stock turnover rate is…
Average debtors R40 000 and credit sales R365 000. The collection period is about…
Compare two partnerships' efficiency.

source_a.text: Source A: stock turnover 8 times; debtors collected in 25 days.

source_b.text: Source B: stock turnover 2 times; debtors collected in 70 days.

statements.text: Has slow-moving stock and slow collections

questions.memo: Source A is efficient; Source B ties up cash in stock and debtors.

questions.question: A very short creditors' payment period may mean the business…
options: Pays suppliers quickly and uses less credit
questions.expected: Pays suppliers quickly and uses less credit
questions.memo: Paying fast reduces the use of supplier credit.

questions.question: High gearing means the business relies heavily on ______ funds.
questions.memo: High gearing means more debt relative to equity.

questions.question: Return on partners' equity measures…
options: Profit earned relative to the partners' equity
questions.expected: Profit earned relative to the partners' equity
questions.memo: ROE relates profit to equity invested.

questions.question: A return on equity higher than the interest rate on savings is good for the partners.
questions.memo: It beats simply leaving the money in the bank.

questions.question: Partners' total earnings include…
options: Salary, interest on capital and profit share
questions.expected: Salary, interest on capital and profit share
questions.memo: Earnings combine salary, interest and profit share.

questions.question: A rising debtors' collection period suggests…
questions.memo: A longer period means slower collection.

questions.question: Compare the gearing of two firms.

statements.text: Relies mostly on its own equity (low risk)
Has a debt-equity ratio that can be assessed

questions.memo: Source A is low-geared and lower risk; Source B is highly geared.

questions.question: A stock holding period of 60 days means stock is held about…
options: Two months before it is sold
questions.expected: Two months before it is sold
questions.memo: 60 days ≈ two months.

questions.question: Comparing this year's ratios to last year's shows the trend.
questions.memo: Trend analysis compares across periods.

questions.question: If gearing is high and profits fall, the partners face…
options: Greater risk, as interest must still be paid
questions.expected: Greater risk, as interest must still be paid
questions.memo: High gearing magnifies risk when profits drop.

questions.question: Why interpret partnership financial statements?
options: To judge profitability, liquidity and risk
questions.expected: To judge profitability, liquidity and risk
questions.memo: Interpretation informs decisions.

questions.question: Return on partners' equity = net profit ÷ ______ × 100.
questions.memo: ROE relates profit to partners' equity.

ACC.G11.T2.CLUBCONCEPTS.A1.title: Clubs (NPO): concepts
ACC.G11.T2.CLUBCONCEPTS.A1.description: Concepts unique to non-profit organisations (clubs): non-profit organisation, constitution, accumulated fund, membership fees, entrance fees, affiliation fees, honorarium, surplus and deficit.
ACC.G11.T2.CLUBCONCEPTS.A1.recovery_strategy: A club has no profit. Its capital is the accumulated fund, and its result for the year is a surplus or deficit, not a profit or loss.

questions.question: A club is a…
questions.memo: Clubs are non-profit organisations.

questions.question: The capital of a club is called the…
questions.memo: A club's 'capital' is the accumulated fund.

questions.question: The rules that govern a club are set out in its ______.
questions.memo: The constitution sets the rules.

questions.question: Money members pay each year to belong is called…
questions.memo: Annual subscriptions are membership fees.

questions.question: A club's main aim is to make a profit for its owners.
questions.memo: A club is non-profit and has no profit-seeking owners.

questions.question: An amount paid to honour someone for voluntary service is an…
questions.memo: An honorarium thanks a volunteer.

questions.question: Sort each item as club income or not income.
questions.memo: Fees and sales are income; a loan received is not income.

questions.question: A club's surplus is similar to a business's…
questions.memo: A surplus is like a profit.

questions.question: A club's deficit is similar to a business's…
questions.memo: A deficit is like a loss.

questions.question: Fees paid once when first joining a club are ______ fees.
questions.memo: Entrance fees are paid on joining.

questions.question: Affiliation fees are paid by a club to…
options: A larger governing body it belongs to
questions.expected: A larger governing body it belongs to
questions.memo: Affiliation fees go to the governing body.

questions.question: Membership fees received in advance are a liability of the club.
questions.memo: Fees for a future period are owed back as service — a liability.

questions.question: Sort each as a receipt or a payment for the club.
questions.memo: Receipts are cash in; payments are cash out.

questions.question: The accumulated fund increases when the club has a…
questions.memo: A surplus is added to the accumulated fund.

questions.question: Why does a club have no ordinary 'capital' account like a business?
options: It has no owner seeking profit; members fund it collectively
questions.expected: It has no owner seeking profit; members fund it collectively
questions.memo: Clubs are member-funded, not owner-funded.

questions.question: Refreshments sold by a club generate ______ for the club.
questions.memo: Refreshment sales are income.

questions.question: A club still keeps proper accounting records.
questions.memo: Non-profit does not mean no records.

questions.question: Membership fees in arrears (still owing by members) are a…
questions.memo: Fees owing to the club are a receivable.

questions.question: The constitution of a club typically sets out…
options: Its aims, fees and how it is run
questions.expected: Its aims, fees and how it is run
questions.memo: It governs the club's purpose and rules.

questions.question: An honorarium is paid to…
options: A volunteer for services, as a token of thanks
questions.expected: A volunteer for services, as a token of thanks
questions.memo: It thanks a volunteer for their service.

ACC.G11.T2.CLUBLEDGER.A1.title: Clubs: cash book, ledger & Statement of Receipts and Payments
ACC.G11.T2.CLUBLEDGER.A1.description: The accounting cycle for clubs: the analysis cash book, posting to the ledger (accumulated fund, membership fees, entrance fees and trading accounts such as refreshments), the Trial Balance, the Statement of Receipts and Payments, and the difference between receipts & income and payments & expenses.
ACC.G11.T2.CLUBLEDGER.A1.recovery_strategy: Receipts and payments are cash movements; income and expenses belong to the period. A loan received is a receipt but not income.

questions.question: The Statement of Receipts and Payments shows the club's…
options: Cash received and paid during the period
questions.expected: Cash received and paid during the period
questions.memo: It summarises the club's cash flows.

questions.question: Receipts and payments are about ______, while income and expenses are about the period.
questions.memo: Receipts and payments track cash movements.

questions.question: A subscription (membership fee) received is recorded as…
questions.memo: Subscriptions are income and a cash receipt.

questions.question: The club receives membership fees in cash.
questions.memo: Fees received: Bank (debit), Membership fees (credit).

questions.question: The club pays wages to its groundsman.
questions.memo: Wages paid: Wages (debit), Bank (credit).

questions.question: Membership fees received for next year are…
questions.memo: Fees for a future year are deferred income.

questions.question: Sort each as a receipt or a payment.
questions.memo: Cash in is a receipt; cash out is a payment.

questions.question: Membership fees still owing by members are fees in ______.
questions.memo: Owing fees are in arrears (a receivable).

questions.question: A surplus for the year is added to the…
questions.memo: Surpluses build the accumulated fund.

questions.question: The club receives a cash donation.
questions.memo: Donation received: Bank (debit), Donations (credit).

questions.question: The difference between receipts and income arises because…
options: Some receipts (e.g. loans) are not income
questions.expected: Some receipts (e.g. loans) are not income
questions.memo: Not every cash receipt is income.

questions.question: A loan received by a club is a receipt but not income.
questions.memo: A loan is cash in but must be repaid — not income.

questions.question: Refreshment sales less refreshment costs gives the club's…
questions.memo: Trading accounts show the result on each activity.

questions.question: Sort each as club income or expense.
questions.memo: Fees and donations received are income; fees and honoraria paid are expenses.

questions.question: The club pays affiliation fees to its governing body.
questions.memo: Affiliation fees paid: Affiliation fees (debit), Bank (credit).

questions.question: The accumulated fund is the club's equivalent of ______.
questions.memo: It plays the role capital does in a business.

questions.question: Membership fees received in advance are shown as a…
questions.memo: Advance fees are a current liability.

questions.question: Entrance fees are usually treated as income of the club.
questions.memo: Entrance fees are income.

questions.question: Why prepare a Statement of Receipts and Payments?
options: To summarise the club's cash flows for the members
questions.expected: To summarise the club's cash flows for the members
questions.memo: It reports cash to members.

questions.question: Subscriptions in arrears at year-end are shown as a…
questions.memo: Owing subscriptions are a receivable.

ACC.G11.T3.COSTCALC.A1.title: Cost accounting: calculations
ACC.G11.T3.COSTCALC.A1.description: Calculating, in a manufacturing environment, variable and fixed costs, the cost of a product using variable and fixed costs, unit cost, contribution per unit and the break-even point.
ACC.G11.T3.COSTCALC.A1.recovery_strategy: Contribution per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit. Break-even units = total fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.

questions.question: Contribution per unit = selling price per unit −…
questions.memo: Contribution = selling price − variable cost per unit.

questions.question: Break-even is the point where total income equals total ______.
questions.memo: At break-even, income exactly covers costs.

questions.question: Fixed costs are costs that…
options: Stay the same in total regardless of output
questions.expected: Stay the same in total regardless of output
questions.memo: Fixed costs do not vary with output.

questions.question: Selling price R50 and variable cost R30 per unit. Contribution per unit is…
Fixed costs R40 000 and contribution per unit R20. Break-even units are…
At the break-even point, the profit is…
questions.memo: Break-even means no profit and no loss.

questions.question: Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per ______.
questions.memo: Divide fixed costs by contribution per unit.

questions.question: Sort each cost as fixed or variable.
questions.memo: Fixed costs stay constant; variable costs change with output.

questions.question: If a business sells more than its break-even units, it makes a…
questions.memo: Beyond break-even, output earns profit.

questions.question: Selling price R80, variable cost R50, fixed costs R60 000. Break-even units are…
questions.memo: Contribution R30; R60 000 ÷ R30 = 2 000 units.

questions.question: Total cost = fixed costs +…
questions.memo: Total cost = fixed + variable costs.

questions.question: Contribution first covers fixed costs, then becomes profit.
questions.memo: Once fixed costs are covered, extra contribution is profit.

questions.question: If the variable cost per unit rises, the break-even point will…
questions.memo: Lower contribution means more units to break even.

questions.question: Selling price − variable cost per unit = ______ per unit.
questions.memo: This difference is the contribution per unit.

questions.question: Fixed costs R90 000, selling price R60, variable cost R30. Break-even units are…
questions.memo: Contribution R30; R90 000 ÷ R30 = 3 000 units.

questions.question: Producing 5 000 units when break-even is 2 000 units means the business is…
questions.memo: Output above break-even yields profit.

questions.question: To lower its break-even point, a business could…
options: Reduce fixed costs or raise the contribution per unit
questions.expected: Reduce fixed costs or raise the contribution per unit
questions.memo: Both lower the break-even quantity.

questions.question: Variable costs per unit usually stay roughly constant as output changes.
questions.memo: Per-unit variable cost is fairly constant; the total changes.

questions.question: Unit cost is the total cost divided by…
questions.memo: Unit cost = total cost ÷ units.

questions.question: Why calculate the break-even point?
options: To know the minimum output needed to avoid a loss
questions.expected: To know the minimum output needed to avoid a loss
questions.memo: It shows the output needed to cover costs.

ACC.G11.T3.MANUFLEDGER.A1.title: Manufacturing ledger accounts
ACC.G11.T3.MANUFLEDGER.A1.description: Preparing the ledger accounts of a manufacturing business: the Balance Sheet section (raw material, work-in-progress, finished goods and consumable stores stock), the nominal accounts section (sales, cost of sales, raw materials issued, factory wages, factory electricity and rent, depreciation) and the cost accounts section (direct materials, direct labour, factory overhead, administration and selling & distribution cost).
ACC.G11.T3.MANUFLEDGER.A1.recovery_strategy: Factory-floor costs are factory overheads; office costs are administration; getting goods to customers is selling & distribution.

questions.question: Raw materials, work-in-progress and finished goods are types of…
questions.memo: They are the three manufacturing stocks.

questions.question: Direct materials + direct labour + factory overheads = ______ cost of production.
questions.memo: Together they give the total cost of production.

questions.question: The wages of factory machine operators are…
questions.memo: Operators' wages are direct labour.

questions.question: Classify each cost.
questions.memo: Each cost belongs to one section of the cost statement.

questions.question: Raw materials are issued from the store to production.
questions.memo: Issuing materials: Raw materials issued (debit), Raw material stock (credit).

questions.question: Factory electricity is classified as a…
questions.memo: Factory power is an overhead.

questions.question: Selling and distribution cost includes…
questions.memo: It covers getting goods to customers.

questions.question: Sort each into Balance Sheet (stock) or Nominal (cost/income).
questions.memo: Stocks are Balance Sheet items; costs and income are nominal.

questions.question: Partly completed goods are ______ stock.
questions.memo: Unfinished goods are work-in-progress.

questions.question: Administration cost includes…
questions.memo: Admin covers office/management costs.

questions.question: Factory wages are paid by EFT.
questions.memo: Factory wages: Factory wages (debit), Bank (credit).

questions.question: The cost of finished goods that are made is transferred to…
questions.memo: Completed goods move to finished goods stock.

questions.question: Direct materials and direct labour together make up the prime cost.
questions.memo: Prime cost = direct materials + direct labour.

questions.question: Which is NOT a manufacturing (factory) cost?
questions.memo: Office salaries are administration, not factory cost.

questions.question: Classify each cost.
questions.memo: Only factory-floor costs are manufacturing costs.

questions.question: Record depreciation on factory equipment.
questions.memo: Depreciation (debit, an overhead); Accumulated depreciation (credit).

questions.question: Raw material, work-in-progress and finished goods stock appear in the…
questions.memo: The three stocks are current assets.

questions.question: Selling and distribution and administration are ______-manufacturing costs.
questions.memo: They are non-manufacturing costs.

questions.question: Consumable stores (indirect materials) are classified as a…
questions.memo: Indirect materials are a factory overhead.

questions.question: Why separate factory costs from administration and selling costs?
options: To calculate the true cost of producing the goods
questions.expected: To calculate the true cost of producing the goods
questions.memo: Accurate product costing needs this split.

ACC.G11.T3.BUDGETING11.A1.title: Budgeting: cash budget & projected income statement
ACC.G11.T3.BUDGETING11.A1.description: Preparing and presenting a cash budget for sole traders (projected receipts and payments, projected debtors' collection and creditors' payments) and a Projected Income Statement (projected revenue and expenditure).
ACC.G11.T3.BUDGETING11.A1.recovery_strategy: The cash budget records cash when it is actually received or paid. Credit sales become receipts only when debtors pay, per the collection pattern.

questions.question: A cash budget plans…
questions.memo: It plans cash in and out.

questions.question: A Projected Income Statement estimates the future…
questions.memo: It forecasts profit.

questions.question: Only ______ items appear in a cash budget.
questions.memo: A cash budget shows actual cash flows only.

questions.question: Depreciation appears in a Projected Income Statement but not in a cash budget.
questions.memo: Depreciation is a non-cash expense.

questions.question: Credit sales appear in the cash budget…
questions.memo: Cash is shown when collected.

questions.question: If 60% of sales are collected in the month of sale, the rest is collected…
questions.memo: The balance follows the collection pattern.

questions.question: Sort each item by whether it appears in the cash budget.
questions.memo: Only real cash flows appear; non-cash items do not.

questions.question: A planned payment to creditors appears in the cash budget in the month…
questions.memo: Cash is shown when paid.

questions.question: Comparing the budget to the ______ figures is a key control.
questions.memo: Budget-to-actual comparison drives control.

questions.question: A favourable cash budget shows…
questions.memo: A surplus means more cash in than out.

questions.question: If the cash budget shows a deficit, the business should plan to…
options: Arrange finance or delay some payments
questions.expected: Arrange finance or delay some payments
questions.memo: Planning ahead manages the shortfall.

questions.question: Bad debts written off appear in the cash budget.
questions.memo: Bad debts are non-cash, so they are excluded.

questions.question: Opening cash balance plus the net cash flow gives the…
questions.memo: Opening + net flow = closing balance.

questions.question: Sort each as a receipt or a payment in the cash budget.
questions.memo: Cash in is a receipt; cash out is a payment.

questions.question: Projected receipts from debtors depend on the…
questions.memo: Collections follow how fast debtors pay.

questions.question: A Projected Income Statement helps predict future ______.
questions.memo: It forecasts the expected profit.

questions.question: Which appears in the Projected Income Statement but NOT the cash budget?
questions.memo: Depreciation is non-cash.

questions.question: A cash budget helps a business avoid running out of cash.
questions.memo: It anticipates shortfalls in advance.

questions.question: Why prepare both a cash budget and a Projected Income Statement?
options: One plans cash, the other plans profit
questions.expected: One plans cash, the other plans profit
questions.memo: They serve different planning needs.

questions.question: Drawings by the owner appear in the cash budget as a…
questions.memo: Drawings are cash paid out.

ACC.G11.T3.INVENTORY11.A1.title: Inventory systems: perpetual vs periodic
ACC.G11.T3.INVENTORY11.A1.description: Defining the perpetual and periodic stock systems, their advantages and disadvantages, and recording transactions under the periodic system compared with the perpetual system: purchases account vs Trading Stock account, opening and closing stock accounts, the Trading Account, carriage on purchases and customs & import duties.
ACC.G11.T3.INVENTORY11.A1.recovery_strategy: Perpetual = stock updated with every transaction (Trading Stock account). Periodic = a Purchases account is used and stock is counted at period-end.

questions.question: Under the perpetual system, the Trading Stock account is updated…
questions.memo: Perpetual = continuous updating.

questions.question: Under the periodic system, purchases are recorded in a…
questions.memo: The periodic system uses a Purchases account.

questions.question: Under the periodic system, stock is counted at the ______ of the period.
questions.memo: A year-end count establishes closing stock.

questions.question: The perpetual system tracks stock continuously.
questions.memo: It updates with each transaction.

questions.question: Carriage on purchases adds to the…
questions.memo: Carriage in is part of stock cost.

questions.question: Match each feature to its system.

items.text: Cost of sales recorded each sale
Stock counted at year-end for cost of sales

questions.memo: Perpetual updates continuously; periodic relies on a year-end count.

questions.question: An advantage of the perpetual system is…
options: Stock levels are known at any time
It is the cheapest to run
questions.expected: Stock levels are known at any time
questions.memo: Continuous records show stock anytime.

questions.question: An advantage of the periodic system is…
options: It is simpler and cheaper to run
Cost of sales is recorded each sale
questions.expected: It is simpler and cheaper to run
questions.memo: Periodic needs less continuous recording.

questions.question: Customs and import duties on goods bought ______ the cost of stock.
questions.memo: Duties add to the cost of the stock.

questions.question: Under the periodic system, cost of sales is found by…
questions.memo: That is the periodic cost-of-sales formula.

questions.question: Under the perpetual system, cost of sales is recorded at the time of each sale.
questions.memo: Each sale records its cost immediately.

questions.question: A disadvantage of the periodic system is…
options: Stock levels are not known between counts
questions.expected: Stock levels are not known between counts
questions.memo: Without continuous records, stock is unknown between counts.

questions.question: Match each account to the system that uses it.
questions.memo: Each system uses different accounts.

questions.question: Opening stock R20 000, purchases R150 000, closing stock R30 000. Cost of sales (periodic) is…
A business with many low-value items might prefer the…
questions.memo: Periodic suits many cheap items.

questions.question: Carriage on purchases is part of the cost of buying stock.
questions.memo: Carriage in adds to stock cost.

questions.question: The perpetual system helps control stock because…
options: It shows expected stock to compare with physical counts
questions.expected: It shows expected stock to compare with physical counts
questions.memo: Comparing records to counts reveals losses.

questions.question: Under the periodic system there is no ______ Stock account updated per transaction.
questions.memo: The periodic system uses Purchases, not a live Trading Stock account.

questions.question: Why might a jewellery shop use the perpetual system?
questions.memo: Valuable goods justify continuous control.

questions.question: Closing stock at year-end is determined by…
questions.memo: A count establishes closing stock.

ACC.G11.T4.VAT11.A1.title: VAT calculations
ACC.G11.T4.VAT11.A1.description: Performing VAT calculations using the current rate: adding VAT to cost price plus mark-up, extracting VAT from a VAT-inclusive amount, working on an invoice or receipt basis, and the effect of bad debts, discounts and goods returned on VAT, with the related ethics and internal control.
ACC.G11.T4.VAT11.A1.recovery_strategy: To ADD VAT: amount × 15%. To EXTRACT VAT from an inclusive amount: amount × 15/115.

questions.question: The standard VAT rate used in calculations is…
questions.memo: The current standard rate is 15%.

questions.question: To add VAT to a VAT-exclusive amount, multiply it by ______%.
questions.memo: VAT = amount × 15%.

questions.question: To find the VAT included in a VAT-inclusive amount, multiply by…
questions.memo: Extract VAT with the 15/115 fraction.

questions.question: VAT is added to cost price plus mark-up to get the VAT-inclusive selling price.
questions.memo: VAT is charged on the selling price.

questions.question: An item costs R200 excluding VAT. The VAT at 15% is…
A VAT-inclusive price is R230. The VAT portion is…
A VAT-inclusive price is R460. The price excluding VAT is…
VAT charged on sales is ______ VAT.
questions.memo: Output VAT is on sales.

questions.question: A business buys stock for R1 150 including VAT. The input VAT it can claim is…
When a customer returns goods, the VAT on those goods is…
questions.memo: Returns reverse the related VAT.

questions.question: A settlement discount reduces both the price and the VAT on it.
questions.memo: Less is charged, so less VAT applies.

questions.question: Cost price R400 with a 50% mark-up. The selling price excluding VAT is…
questions.memo: R400 + 50% = R600 (before VAT).

questions.question: Selling price excluding VAT is R600. The VAT-inclusive price is…
VAT paid on purchases is ______ VAT.
questions.memo: Input VAT is on purchases.

questions.question: VAT payable to SARS = output VAT −…
questions.memo: Net VAT = output − input VAT.

questions.question: An amount of R1 725 includes VAT. The VAT portion is…
Charging VAT but not paying it over to SARS is illegal and unethical.
questions.memo: Withholding collected VAT is VAT fraud.

questions.question: When a debt is written off as bad, the business may…
options: Claim back the output VAT it had paid on that sale
questions.expected: Claim back the output VAT it had paid on that sale
questions.memo: Bad debts allow a VAT adjustment.

questions.question: Good internal control over VAT ensures the correct amount is paid to ______.
questions.memo: Proper control gets the right amount to SARS.

questions.question: Why must a vendor keep accurate VAT records?
options: To pay SARS the right amount and claim valid input VAT
questions.expected: To pay SARS the right amount and claim valid input VAT
questions.memo: Accurate records ensure correct VAT.

ACC.G12.T1.COCONCEPTS.A1.title: Companies: concepts & unique accounts
ACC.G12.T1.COCONCEPTS.A1.description: Concepts unique to companies: public and private companies, the Companies Act, the Registrar of Companies, the Memorandum of Incorporation, income tax and provisional tax, dividends, shares, issue price, earnings, shareholders, directors, auditors, limited liability, the separation of ownership from control, retained income, authorised and issued share capital and the JSE.
ACC.G12.T1.COCONCEPTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Authorised = the maximum number of shares the company MAY issue. Issued = the shares actually sold to shareholders.

questions.question: A company is owned by its…
questions.memo: Companies are owned by shareholders.

questions.question: The maximum number of shares a company may issue is its…
questions.memo: Authorised capital is the ceiling on shares.

questions.question: Shares actually sold to shareholders are the…
questions.memo: Issued capital is the shares actually sold.

questions.question: Profit kept in the company and not paid out is ______ income.
questions.memo: Undistributed profit is retained income.

questions.question: Shareholders have limited liability.
questions.memo: Their loss is limited to what they invested.

questions.question: A portion of profit paid out to shareholders is a…
questions.memo: Dividends distribute profit to shareholders.

questions.question: Sort each term by whether it belongs to a company.
questions.memo: Shareholders and dividends are company terms; members and partners are not.

questions.question: The separation of ownership from control means…
options: Shareholders own the company but directors manage it
questions.expected: Shareholders own the company but directors manage it
questions.memo: Owners appoint directors to manage.

questions.question: A public company's shares can be…
questions.memo: Public company shares trade on the JSE.

questions.question: The document setting out a company's rules is the Memorandum of ______.
questions.memo: The MOI governs the company.

questions.question: Directors are…
options: Appointed to manage the company for the shareholders
The owners of all the shares
questions.expected: Appointed to manage the company for the shareholders
questions.memo: Directors manage on behalf of shareholders.

questions.question: A private company's shares are freely traded on the stock exchange.
questions.memo: Private company shares are not freely traded.

questions.question: A company's income tax is paid to…
questions.memo: Company tax is paid to SARS.

questions.question: Sort each into authorised or issued share capital.

items.text: Maximum shares the company may issue

questions.memo: Authorised is the ceiling; issued is what has been sold.

questions.question: Limited liability protects shareholders by…
options: Limiting their loss to the amount they invested
questions.expected: Limiting their loss to the amount they invested
questions.memo: They can lose only their investment.

questions.question: The auditors of a company…
options: Give an independent opinion on the financial statements
questions.expected: Give an independent opinion on the financial statements
questions.memo: External auditors express an opinion.

questions.question: Authorised capital is the ______ number of shares the company may issue.
questions.memo: It is the ceiling on shares.

questions.question: Retained income belongs to the shareholders.
questions.memo: Retained income is shareholders' undistributed profit.

questions.question: The JSE is…
options: The Johannesburg Securities Exchange, where shares are traded
questions.expected: The Johannesburg Securities Exchange, where shares are traded
questions.memo: The JSE is South Africa's stock exchange.

questions.question: Why does a company separate ownership from control?
options: Many shareholders cannot all manage, so directors do it for them
questions.expected: Many shareholders cannot all manage, so directors do it for them
questions.memo: Directors manage on behalf of dispersed owners.

ACC.G12.T1.COBOOKKEEPING.A1.title: Companies: bookkeeping
ACC.G12.T1.COBOOKKEEPING.A1.description: The accounting cycle for a company, including issuing shares at issue price (no par value or share premium under the Companies Act), buying back shares, loans and interest (mortgage interest capitalised), income tax, dividends, directors' fees and audit fees.
ACC.G12.T1.COBOOKKEEPING.A1.recovery_strategy: Dividends are a distribution of profit, not an expense. They are appropriated after profit, not deducted in the Income Statement.

questions.question: When a company issues shares for cash, the bank increases and…
questions.memo: Issuing shares raises share capital.

questions.question: Dividends are a ______ of profit, not an expense.
questions.memo: Dividends distribute profit.

questions.question: Directors' fees are…
questions.memo: Directors' fees are an expense.

questions.memo: Issuing shares: Bank (debit), Ordinary share capital (credit).

questions.question: The company pays an interim dividend by EFT.
questions.memo: Paying a dividend: Dividends (debit), Bank (credit).

questions.memo: Audit fees: Audit fees (debit), Bank (credit).

questions.question: The company provides for the income tax for the year.
questions.memo: Provision for tax: Income tax (debit), SARS (income tax) (credit).

questions.question: Buying back its own shares causes the company's share capital to…
questions.memo: A share buy-back reduces share capital.

questions.question: Interest on a mortgage loan is ______ (added to the loan).
questions.memo: Mortgage interest is capitalised.

questions.question: Sort each item by how it is treated.
questions.memo: Fees are expenses; dividends distribute profit.

questions.question: Audit fees are paid to the…
questions.memo: Audit fees go to the external auditors.

questions.question: When shares are issued, the price received per share is the…
questions.memo: Shares are issued at the issue price.

questions.question: Under the Companies Act, shares no longer have a par value.
questions.memo: Par value and share premium were removed.

questions.question: The company issues additional shares and receives the cash.
questions.memo: More shares issued: Bank (debit), Ordinary share capital (credit).

questions.question: Directors' fees differ from dividends because directors' fees are…
options: Payment for managing, not a share of profit
questions.expected: Payment for managing, not a share of profit
questions.memo: Fees pay directors for their work.

questions.question: Repurchasing shares reduces both…
options: The bank and the share capital
questions.expected: The bank and the share capital
questions.memo: Cash is paid and capital falls.

questions.question: Company profits are taxed; the tax is paid to ______.
questions.memo: Company income tax is paid to SARS.

questions.question: The company pays the directors' fees by EFT.
questions.memo: Directors' fees: Directors' fees (debit), Bank (credit).

questions.question: A loan and the interest on it are recorded as…
options: A liability and an expense respectively
questions.expected: A liability and an expense respectively
questions.memo: The loan is a liability; interest is an expense.

questions.question: Why are dividends not shown as an expense?
options: They distribute profit already earned, not a cost of earning it
questions.expected: They distribute profit already earned, not a cost of earning it
questions.memo: Dividends share profit, they do not create it.

ACC.G12.T1.COADJUSTMENTS.A1.title: Companies: adjustments & final accounts

ACC.G12.T1.COADJUSTMENTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Company profit is taxed: account for income tax to reach profit after tax, then appropriate dividends and retained income.

questions.question: Company income tax is calculated on the company's…
questions.memo: Tax is based on taxable profit.

questions.question: Profit after tax is shared as dividends and ______ income.

questions.question: A dividend declared but not yet paid is a…
questions.memo: Shareholders for dividends is a current liability.

questions.question: Provide for the income tax for the year.
questions.memo: Tax provision: Income tax (debit), SARS (income tax) (credit).

questions.question: Declare a final dividend that is not yet paid.
questions.memo: Declaring a dividend: Dividends (debit), Shareholders for dividends (credit).

questions.question: Provide for income tax owing at year-end.
questions.memo: The tax expense reduces equity; the amount owing to SARS is a liability.

questions.question: Declare a dividend that is not yet paid.
questions.memo: The dividend reduces retained income (equity); the amount owed to shareholders is a liability.

questions.question: Pay the previously declared dividend by EFT.
questions.memo: Bank (asset) falls; the dividend liability is settled.

questions.question: The Appropriation Account of a company shows…
options: Income tax, dividends and retained income
questions.expected: Income tax, dividends and retained income
questions.memo: It appropriates after-tax profit.

questions.question: Net profit after tax less dividends equals the change in ______ income.
questions.memo: What is not distributed is retained.

questions.question: Write off depreciation for the year.
questions.memo: Depreciation (debit); Accumulated depreciation (credit).

questions.question: Interest on a mortgage loan is…
questions.memo: Mortgage interest is capitalised.

questions.question: Increase the provision for bad debts at year-end.
questions.memo: Net debtors fall; the increase is an expense reducing equity.

questions.question: A provision for bad debts…
options: Reduces the net debtors shown in the Balance Sheet
questions.expected: Reduces the net debtors shown in the Balance Sheet
questions.memo: It is netted against debtors.

questions.question: Dividends are appropriated from profit after tax.
questions.memo: Dividends come out of after-tax profit.

questions.question: If a company makes a loss, it generally pays…
options: No income tax for that year
questions.expected: No income tax for that year
questions.memo: No taxable profit means no income tax.

questions.memo: The expense reduces equity; the amount owing is a liability.

questions.memo: Tax reduces the profit available to shareholders.

questions.question: Reversals at the start of the new year apply to…
options: Accruals, prepayments and income received in advance
questions.expected: Accruals, prepayments and income received in advance
questions.memo: These timing adjustments are reversed.

questions.question: Why must income tax be accounted for before dividends?
options: Dividends are paid from after-tax profit
questions.expected: Dividends are paid from after-tax profit
questions.memo: Tax comes first; dividends follow from what remains.

ACC.G12.T1.COSTATEMENTS.A1.title: Companies: financial statements & Cash Flow Statement

questions.question: The Cash Flow Statement (unique to companies) shows…
options: How cash moved during the year
questions.expected: How cash moved during the year
questions.memo: It explains the change in cash.

questions.question: The three sections of the Cash Flow Statement are operating, investing and…
questions.memo: The three sections are operating, investing and financing.

questions.question: Cash from day-to-day trading appears under ______ activities.
questions.memo: Trading cash flows are operating activities.

questions.question: Buying or selling fixed assets appears under…
questions.memo: Asset purchases/sales are investing activities.

questions.question: Issuing shares or raising loans appears under financing activities.
questions.memo: Raising capital is a financing activity.

questions.question: Sort each cash flow into the correct section.
questions.memo: Trading is operating; assets are investing; shares/loans/dividends are financing.

questions.question: The Income Statement of a company is also called the…
questions.memo: The IFRS name is the Statement of Comprehensive Income.

questions.question: The Balance Sheet of a company is also called the…
questions.memo: The IFRS name is the Statement of Financial Position.

questions.question: Proceeds from a new loan are a ______ activity.
questions.memo: Raising a loan is a financing activity.

questions.question: Which is the correct order in the Cash Flow Statement?
options: Operating → Investing → Financing → Net change in cash

questions.question: Which appears under operating activities?
questions.memo: Customer receipts are operating cash flows.

questions.question: In the Cash Flow Statement, depreciation is…
options: Added back to profit (it is non-cash)
questions.expected: Added back to profit (it is non-cash)
questions.memo: Depreciation is added back as it used no cash.

questions.question: Sort each item by which statement it appears in.
questions.memo: Each figure belongs to a particular statement.

questions.question: The Cash Flow Statement explains the change in the company's cash over the year.
questions.memo: It reconciles opening to closing cash.

questions.question: A company with good profit but poor cash flow might have…
options: Much profit tied up in stock or debtors
questions.expected: Much profit tied up in stock or debtors
questions.memo: Profit can be locked up in working capital.

questions.question: Dividends paid are shown under ______ activities in the Cash Flow Statement.
questions.memo: Dividends paid are a financing outflow.

questions.question: Notes to the financial statements…
options: Give detail supporting the statement figures
questions.expected: Give detail supporting the statement figures
questions.memo: Notes explain the figures.

questions.question: Buying fixed assets appears as a/an…
questions.memo: Cash spent on assets is an investing outflow.

questions.question: The three financial statements together give a fuller picture than any one alone.
questions.memo: Each statement shows a different dimension.

questions.question: Why does a company prepare a Cash Flow Statement?
options: To show where cash came from and how it was used
questions.expected: To show where cash came from and how it was used
questions.memo: It reports the sources and uses of cash.

ACC.G12.T1.COINTERPRET.A1.title: Companies: analysis & interpretation
ACC.G12.T1.COINTERPRET.A1.description: Analysing and interpreting the Income Statement, Balance Sheet and notes, including the earlier indicators plus debt-equity ratio (gearing), return on shareholders' equity, return on total capital employed, net asset value per share, dividends per share and earnings per share.

questions.question: Earnings per share (EPS) measures…
questions.memo: EPS = profit after tax per issued share.

questions.question: Dividends per share (DPS) measures…
questions.memo: DPS = dividends per issued share.

questions.question: Net asset value per share shows the ______ behind each share.
questions.memo: NAV per share is net assets per share.

questions.question: Return on shareholders' equity shows the return earned for the owners.
questions.memo: ROSHE relates profit to shareholders' equity.

questions.question: Net profit after tax R500 000 and 1 000 000 shares in issue. EPS is…

questions.memo: Gearing compares debt to equity.

questions.memo: Higher EPS means more profit per share.

questions.question: Why interpret a company's financial statements?

questions.question: Earnings per share = net profit after tax ÷…
questions.memo: EPS divides after-tax profit by issued shares.

ACC.G12.T1.COPUBLISHED.A1.title: Analysis of published statements & audit reports

questions.question: A company's published annual report includes the…

questions.question: A qualified audit report means…

questions.question: The Directors' Report mainly reports on…
